World.title: Czech Fish Farmers Take Emergency Measures Amid Prolonged Drought
World.content:
Fish farmers reduce or suspend supplementary feeding to lower oxygen consumption, reports say.

Fish farmers in the Czech Republic have begun taking emergency measures as a prolonged drought, worsened by high temperatures across Europe, strains water supplies.

Facing water shortages, fish farmers have reduced or suspended supplementary feeding to lower fish oxygen consumption, while ponds are being regularly aerated, according to the report.



Several ponds have also been netted earlier than usual.

In the Třeboň area, which delivers tons of carp for the Czech Christmas table, part of the 200-hectare Koclířov pond has been drained and the fish moved to holding tanks.

More than a third of the water is missing from the region’s famous system of fish ponds due to the drought. The water level in Lake Svět, for example, has fallen by 98 centimetres. High temperatures are also causing water to evaporate more quickly.

The Czech government is expected to address the 2027 budget, upcoming elections and measures to tackle worsening drought.

Prime Minister Andrej Babiš has pledged an extra CZK 4 billion for drought-related measures. If approved, ministers will present plans for implementing them.

World.title: Burgermeister to Open First Prague Restaurant on Wenceslas Square in 2027
World.content:
Berlin burger chain Burgermeister is preparing to enter the Czech market, with its first Prague restaurant expected to open in early 2027.

The company has chosen Wenceslas Square for its debut. The location will also serve as a base for Burgermeister’s planned expansion across the Czech Republic, with more restaurants already in the pipeline.

Burgermeister has built its reputation in Berlin over the past two decades, growing from a single restaurant in a former public toilet into an international chain with 32 locations across Germany and other European markets.



Burgermeister has not yet revealed the exact address or confirmed a specific opening date.

The Prague restaurant will follow the concept that made Burgermeister popular in Berlin. The chain focuses on freshly prepared burgers and fries, with part of its food production handled in-house. Its operations also include its own bakery.

From a former public toilet to an international burger chain

Burgermeister opened its first restaurant in the Kreuzberg district of Berlin in 2006. The location was far from a conventional restaurant site. It occupied a former public toilet beneath the railway tracks near Schlesisches Tor station.

The unusual setting quickly became part of the brand’s identity. Over the years, Burgermeister expanded beyond its original Berlin location and developed into a larger restaurant chain.

Today, the company has 32 branches and is pursuing its goal of building a pan-European network.

World.title: Russell Crowe to Perform in Prague for the First Time in May 2027
World.content:
Oscar-winning actor and musician Russell Crowe will bring his band, The Gentlemen Barbers, to Forum Karlín on May 23, 2027, for their first-ever Prague concert.

Russell Crowe is best known for his roles in Gladiator, A Beautiful Mind and A Good Year, but long before Hollywood, music was a major part of his life.

On May 23, 2027, the Oscar and Golden Globe winner will bring that side of his career to Prague for the first time, performing with his band The Gentlemen Barbers at Forum Karlín.



Tickets will go on sale soon via Ticketportal and Ticketmaster.

The concert will also mark the opening night of the band’s European tour.

The Gentlemen Barbers have been developing their sound over the past four years, although many of the musicians have worked with Crowe for decades. The lineup includes drummer Dave Kelly and trumpeter Stewart Kirwan, both former members of Thirty Odd Foot of Grunts, as well as musicians who have collaborated with Crowe on later projects.

The band also features pianist Stu Hunter, guitarist Chris Kamzelas and bassist James Hazelwood. Irish singer Lorraine O’Reilly, known for her powerful, raspy vocals, has performed with Crowe since they first met while recording a duet for the Bible Code Sundays album Walk Like Kings.

The result is a band that moves between R&B, gospel, country, dark waltzes and singalong anthems, with storytelling at the centre of its music.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by JV Classics (@jvclassics)

“There is an attitude about this band. It’s got a groove. We do a lot of story songs, but we also know we are here to blow out cobwebs and give the audience a good night,” Crowe says.

For Crowe, music has remained a constant alongside his film career. He began performing in bands, touring and releasing records before moving into musical theatre and eventually film. He has continued to perform throughout his decades in Hollywood, despite his demanding acting career.

“I love playing in pubs. It’s what I did growing up. Even though my day job has a huge claim on my time, I’ve never not played music,” he says.

Russell Crowe’s Indoor Garden Party & The Gentlemen Barbers takes place on May 23, 2027, at 8 p.m. at Forum Karlín in Prague.

World.title: How Much Can a Prague Taxi Driver Really Earn Each Month
World.content:
For passengers, a taxi ride can make the job look straightforward. Pick someone up, drive them across Prague, wait for the next booking and repeat.

But the income of a full-time taxi driver depends on far more than the fare shown on the meter or app.

Drivers working through platforms such as Uber and Bolt can generate more than CZK 60,000 in gross monthly revenue when working around 40 to 50 hours a week. What they actually keep, however, is considerably less.



Gross income can exceed CZK 60,000

Official figures for Prague’s taxi sector put the average gross monthly pay at roughly CZK 38,000. Drivers who work full time through ride-hailing platforms can earn more, particularly when they concentrate on periods of high demand.

According to Ondřej Krátký, founder of the Czech taxi platform Liftago, drivers can typically earn about CZK 250 to CZK 350 per hour. At the lower end of the market, however, some drivers make only around CZK 80 an hour, which is difficult to turn into a sustainable income in Prague.

Official statistics may also underestimate the money generated by some drivers because not every journey is paid through an app. Cash payments remain part of the business.

Fuel and commissions take a large share

Most Prague taxi drivers operate as self-employed contractors and use their own cars. That means they are responsible for almost all of the costs associated with the job.

Fuel is one of the largest expenses. Someone driving every day can spend more than CZK 10,000 a month on petrol or diesel alone.

Ride-hailing platforms also take a percentage of each fare. Depending on the service and other conditions, commissions can account for roughly 20 to 25 percent of the fare. Drivers must also cover vehicle maintenance, repairs, commercial insurance and the mandatory social and health insurance payments required of self-employed workers.

Once these expenses are taken into account, the amount left from gross earnings can fall by a third or more.

For a full-time driver, a realistic monthly amount after operating costs can therefore be somewhere between CZK 22,000 and CZK 35,000. The exact figure depends on the car, fuel consumption, working hours, platform commissions and the number and type of trips completed.

Tips make only a small difference

Tips are unlikely to transform a taxi driver’s income in the Czech Republic.

Unlike in countries where tipping is a major part of service workers’ earnings, Czech passengers generally round up the fare or leave a relatively small amount.

Uber allows passengers to tip through its app for up to 30 days after a journey, with the full tip going to the driver. Bolt offers a similar feature.

For most drivers, however, tips remain a minor addition to their monthly income rather than a significant source of earnings.

Timing can make a bigger difference

Drivers can increase their income by choosing when and where they work.

Friday and Saturday nights are among the busiest periods in Prague, particularly in the city centre. When demand rises sharply, ride-hailing platforms can increase fares, allowing drivers to generate more revenue from the same number of working hours.

Major concerts, festivals and other large events can have a similar effect. Airport journeys can also be attractive because they tend to cover longer distances than short trips within the city.

World.title: Czechia Now Ranks Among the World’s 10 Best Countries to Live In
World.content:
Czechia has placed ninth among 192 countries in the 2026 Rumavi Global Relocation Index, which assesses destinations based on factors including safety, healthcare, taxation, living costs and opportunities for people considering a move abroad.

The country scored 69.9 points in the overall ranking, putting it just outside the top five but ahead of Malta and several larger European economies. Estonia took first place with 72.8 points, followed by Singapore, Malaysia, Portugal and Taiwan.

Czechia performed particularly well in the ranking for families, where it placed third worldwide. The index also gave the country strong scores for safety, property rights and climate risk.



Within Europe, Czechia ranked fourth overall. Estonia, Portugal and Lithuania were the only European countries placed higher in the general ranking.

The results are based on the Rumavi Global Relocation Index 2026, a privately produced ranking designed for people considering relocation as well as investors. Rumavi evaluates 192 countries using 24 indicators grouped into four areas: finance and taxes, livability and health, safety and stability, and settling and opportunity.

Czechia scores particularly well for families

The index uses different weightings for different types of people considering a move. For families, safety, education, cost of living and healthcare carry greater weight than tax considerations.

Czechia’s overall result is less impressive for other groups. It ranked 20th among countries assessed for retirees and 25th for digital nomads.

The index also evaluates destinations for entrepreneurs and people primarily interested in tax efficiency, although the rankings can vary significantly depending on the category.

What the index measures

Rumavi says its ranking is intended to measure the practical conditions faced by someone moving to another country rather than simply assessing tourism or passport access.

The 24 indicators cover issues such as affordability, income tax, foreign-income taxation, banking, healthcare, housing, air quality, climate, digital infrastructure, education, business opportunities, language, visa access, property rights and startup ecosystems.

Each indicator is converted to a score between zero and 100, with higher scores representing more favorable conditions for someone relocating. The same data is then weighted differently for six groups: general applicants, retirees, digital nomads, families, entrepreneurs and people seeking tax advantages.

For the general ranking, the most heavily weighted indicators include street safety, foreign-income taxation, cost of living and climate comfort.

Rumavi’s methodology draws on sources including the World Bank, World Health Organization, OECD, World Justice Project, UNODC and other international datasets. Some indicators, including visa access, property rights for non-citizens and aspects of taxation, are classified as Rumavi assessments rather than direct institutional data.

World.title: Passenger Attacks Four Airport Staff After Being Denied Boarding in Prague
World.content:
A passenger attacked four employees of ground-handling company Menzies Aviation at Prague’s Airport on Thursday evening after being denied boarding on a flight to Rome.

The incident took place at Terminal 2, near Gate C9, shortly after 8 p.m., according to Zdopravy.cz.

The woman arrived late for boarding on a Ryanair flight. After being refused entry to the aircraft, she reportedly became aggressive and attacked members of the ground-handling staff.



One of the employees stepped between the woman and a colleague who was being confronted by her. The passenger then bit him.

Airport police were called to the scene and used restraint equipment to detain the woman. She was subsequently escorted from the boarding area and handed over to the Czech police.

“The woman was late for the boarding gate, and after being denied boarding, she physically attacked an airport employee,” Josef Urban, a spokesperson for the Foreign Police Directorate said.

“Responding officers detained her using restraint equipment, and the case is now being investigated as disorderly conduct,” he added.

The incident was also confirmed by Prague Airport spokesperson Jiří Hánich.

The injured employees required medical treatment following the attack. Four members of the Menzies team were reportedly involved in the incident.

Menzies Aviation has operated at Václav Havel Airport Prague since 1991. The company provides ground-handling services covering passengers, baggage, aircraft and cargo for a significant share of flights at the airport.

World.title: Around 300 Czech Citizens Evacuated Due to Fire in Croatia
World.content:
Some 300 Czech tourists are among the 1,000 evacuees with a Czech police officer sent to coordinate the emergency response.

Croatian prime minister Andrej Plenković is in the town holding a coordination meeting with all emergency services this morning. Croatian president Zoran Milanović is also expected later today.

“All those injured in last night’s fire are being provided with the necessary medical care,” Plenković said in an earlier update on X.

No fatalities have been reported. The spokesman said there were also no reports of serious injuries among Czech citizens.

Some tourists left the area on their own, while others are staying at evacuation centres in Omiš and Split. A Czech consul is on site and is in contact with local authorities and security forces.

Fire spreads across up to 1,000 hectares

Around 160 firefighters, supported by specialised firefighting aircraft, are battling the blaze.

The fire has caused significant material damage, according to eyewitnesses, with dozens of cars and homes reportedly destroyed. Strong winds have helped the flames spread across an area estimated at between 900 and 1,000 hectares.

Witnesses reported hearing gas cylinders exploding inside burning homes, while the streets were filled with the sirens of fire engines, ambulances and police vehicles. Large parts of Omiš have also been left without electricity.

Mass evacuation underway

Hundreds of people have fled the affected area, with some tourists escaping by boat, catamaran and other small vessels.

The organised evacuation is being coordinated through the Ribnjak sports hall in Omiš. From there, evacuees are being transported by bus to the Gripe sports centre in Split.

According to Omiš fire chief Slavko Tucaković, foreigners make up the majority of those evacuated.

World.title: Czech Villages Face Water Shortages as Drought Deepens
World.content:
Residents say they are cutting water use wherever possible, taking shorter showers, reducing garden watering and abandoning plans to fill swimming pool.

Communities across the Czech Republic are struggling with worsening water shortages as wells dry up and small streams disappear after years of increasingly severe drought, according to local media on Thursday.



In the village of Krsy in the Plzen Region, tankers are delivering drinking water daily to a reservoir above the village. Some private wells have already run dry, while others are close to empty.

Residents said they are cutting water use wherever possible, taking shorter showers, reducing garden watering and abandoning plans to fill swimming pools.

Authorities are urging households to connect to public water networks where available.

The shortages are also putting pressure on tourist destinations. In Horni Becva, in the Beskydy Mountains, the population doubles during the summer holidays.

The municipality’s two wells have been operating close to their limits, with firefighters called in to deliver water.

Hotels with wellness facilities are among the largest users, prompting local officials to ask businesses to reduce consumption.

Officials hope conditions will improve when the tourist season ends and autumn rains arrive.

World.title: Could the August 20 fireworks be cancelled? Looming peril threatens Budapest
World.content:
As the August 20 fireworks approach, forecast uncertainty invariably rises, for late summer brings a confluence of atmospheric influences to the Carpathian Basin. This volatility, coupled with the sudden onset of violent showers and thunderstorms, could place the national day celebrations in jeopardy. There is precedent: a few years ago the display was called off over fears of an approaching storm, while in 2006 an inhuman gale that broke during the fireworks themselves left five dead and hundreds injured.

Forecasting August 20 remains notoriously difficult

The Carpathian Basin’s hitherto monotonous summer weather is now shifting. This morning, a continuous cloud layer obscured the sun over Budapest, and a brief shower drenched the capital and its environs in the small hours. For weeks there had been no rain to speak of, nor even cloudy skies; a scorching heatwave had baked Hungary and the surrounding region.

Storms after heatwave. Photo: Anadolu/Németi Róbert

A significant atmospheric reorganisation is under way, yet the heat is not retreating – and that combination may render the national holiday genuinely hazardous. Cool, 12–22°C dawns will be followed by daytime highs of 30–35°C, conditions that readily spawn violent showers and thunderstorms. The meteorological service has therefore issued lemon-yellow warnings for several counties, as reported by Blikk. Precisely what to expect on Thursday remains exceptionally difficult to predict.

On multiple occasions, forecasters have only been able to confirm at the last moment that no major storm would materialise; conversely, events have been cancelled on the basis of such warnings.

Ominous precedents

In 2022, for example, forecasts indicated a serious storm threatening the capital. When the prediction ultimately proved erroneous, the Government dismissed the then president and deputy president of the National Meteorological Service. The fireworks were held a week later, on August 27.On August 20, 2006, however, the display was not called off in time. A storm arriving with winds of 120 km/h struck the celebrating capital. Five people died and more than 300 were injured; the Orbán government in 2022 was determined to avoid any repeat of that catastrophe.

Photo: Facebook/Magyarország Kormánya

If you missed: ‘People were shouting, trapped beneath the seats’ – exclusive interview, video and latest developments in Polish bus crash

A radical shift in Hungary’s weather

At present, meteorologists are expecting partly cloudy, sunny conditions on August 20, but showers and thunderstorms could break out almost anywhere owing to the persistent heat and elevated mean temperatures.

According to an analysis by The Weather on Maps, the heatwave-inducing air mass is drifting eastwards and weakening, while a cool oceanic–Arctic air mass is advancing; their frontal boundary will undulate over our region, definitively ending the recent weather monotony. This, however, introduces another uncertainty factor for the fireworks. It is also the change that may bring more substantial rainfall to the upper catchment of the Danube and thus assist Paks.

Ongoing heroic work near the Paks NPP to raise the water level of the drying Danube and provide enough cooling water for the plant. Photo: Facebook/Péter Magyar

On the national holiday, therefore, everyone would do well to keep abreast of the expected weather – and then no one should be caught unawares.

World.title: PM Magyar’s stern message to richest Hungarian Lőrinc Mészáros over scheme to aid very poor, but high-achieving students
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar called on MBH Bank and Lőrinc Mészáros, who has ties to business interests with stakes in the lender, to reinstate a charity programme benefitting children from low-income households with good grades in a post on Facebook on Monday.

New HQ of Lőrinc Mészáros’s bank too expensive?

Magyar said that the International Children’s Safety Service had announced that MBH Bank had pulled support for the programme, after 32 years, while moving forward with the construction of a new corporate headquarters, “in an untransparent manner”, at a cost of more than HUF 100bn.

Lőrinc Mészáros and former FM Péter Szijjártó. The latter is now a top executive of the Chinese BYD. Photo: FB/Szijjártó

In the name of the state of Hungary, which is also a stakeholder in MBH Bank, Magyar called on Mészáros and MBH Bank to publish the details of the new HQ, including the plans and the name of the general contractor, MTI wrote.

MBH Bank, Hungary’s second-largest commercial lender, is listed on the Budapest Stock Exchange. A little more than 25pc of the bank’s shares are in free float.

Péter Magyar wrote in a Facebook post that Mészáros’s bank had helped 100 low‑income, high‑achieving students under a programme it now plans to cancel.

Hungary’s richest reshaped by the Orbán era: Mészáros wealth surges by 284,400% in 15 years!

The bank responded

The scholarship was open to outstanding students from families whose per‑capita monthly income was below HUF 55,000 (about €151). Recipients received HUF 800,000 a year (roughly €2,200), equivalent to around €183 per month.The bank’s full‑year profit for 2025 stood at HUF 240 billion (€661 million).

In response to a statement by the International Children’s Safety Service, the bank said it was “baffled” that the organisation had taken the matter to the press. MBH Bank stated that its decision to withdraw from the programme had been made last year and that the organisation had been given a year to prepare for the consequences. The bank did not respond directly to Péter Magyar’s remarks, but added that it had spent “tens of millions of forints” on the scheme in recent years.

World.title: Details emerge for this year’s August 20 celebrations: beer prices, performers, concerts – and PM Magyar moonlighting as a DJ?
World.content:
Just as on May 9 at his inauguration, PM Péter Magyar is expected to take his place once more behind the DJ decks on Kossuth Square, in front of the Hungarian Parliament. Yet the August 20 celebrations for Hungary’s National Day will not be confined to this central stage: parties are also planned in front of the Technical University and on Margaret Island. And, reassuringly for revellers, beer will not be prohibitively expensive. The details follow.

End of generous subsidies on August 20

According to the latest information from Telex, discounted beer prices will once again feature at this year’s August 20 celebrations in Budapest – though they will be considerably higher than last year’s. In previous years, the Orbán governments took great care to ensure that certain products remained exceptionally cheap during the national day festivities. Thus, draught Borsodi (0.4l) could be had for as little as 380 forints, while a canned version (0.5l) cost 430 forints. Wine was also inexpensive (260 forints per decilitre), as were pálinka, mineral water, Viennese pretzels and Coca-Cola or Pepsi.

August 20 celebrations in Budapest before. Photo: FB

This year, however, the new government is no longer subsidising these prices so generously, meaning costs will rise significantly – albeit still below full market rates. The reason is that, while there is no direct subsidy, a price cap remains in place: no vendor will be permitted to sell beer for more than 1,000 forints or mineral water for more than 500 forints.

These terms were set by the event organiser, Centrum Production. Partly due to the absence of state price support, the celebration itself will be considerably cheaper to stage: the Tisza government intends to run the entire affair on a budget of just 4 billion forints.

The military show is a traditional part of the August 20 celebrations. Source: FB/Hungarian Government

A shorter fireworks display – and DJ Péter Magyar?

In return, even the traditionally spectacular fireworks will be briefer. The fireworks, held every year since the 1930s, will not be cancelled this year, but will last only 10 minutes. By way of contrast, last year’s display ran for 30 minutes, commissioned by the then government with a pronounced focus on King Peter Orseolo, one of Saint Stephen’s successors (1038–1041; 1044–1046), implicitly drawing an unflattering parallel between that controversial figure and the then opposition leader, now Prime Minister, Péter Magyar.

Alongside the fireworks and the pricier beer, there will be numerous free, open-air events on August 19 and 20 across three venues. On both days, the Danube embankment in front of the Technical University will host Elektro Rakpart, featuring a host of performers, while Kossuth Square will transform into Diszkótér, with acts including Anima Sound System.

The traditional fireworks over Budapest: this year it will be cheaper and shorter. Photo: Facebook/Magyarország Kormánya

Whether Péter Magyar will again step behind the DJ console – as he did on May 9 at his inauguration – remains a mystery. What is certain, according to Telex, is that a number of surprise guests have yet to be announced.

Traffic changed due to the 20 August celebrations – check out the details in our article

On Margaret Island, alternative music and guitars will take centre stage on both days. Among the acts scheduled to appear are Quimby, and there will also be an LGT tribute concert courtesy of Random Trip. For full details, readers are directed to the Telex article.

August 20 celebrations: what for?

August 20 is Hungary’s red-letter day, the nation’s official state holiday, commemorating the foundation of the state and Saint Stephen, the first Christian king of Hungary. King Stephen, canonised in 1083 (reigned 997/1000–1038), continued the state- and church-building “work” of his father, Grand Prince Géza (972–997), integrating Hungary into the Christian European world. To this end, he overcame rival claimants to the throne and domestic opponents, while also successfully repelling external interference. By the end of his reign, Hungary was a young state with a solid administrative structure, firmly part of Christian Europe – one that successfully weathered the turbulent decades following Stephen’s death (1038–1046).

The portrait of St Stephen made by an unnamed artist who could see the king with his own eyes more than a millenium ago – read our article to find out where you can check it out. Photo: Creative Commons

Major changes are coming to Hungary’s 20 August celebrations this year: here’s what’s in store

World.title: Invasive mosquito species conquering Hungary – climate change destroys our echosystem?
World.content:
Drought has driven native mosquitoes from much of Hungary, only for invasive species—chiefly the Asian tiger mosquito—to thrive in residential areas, the National Directorate General for Disaster Management (OKF) has warned.

Mosquito patterns shaped by drought

Across most of the country, dry weather continues to dictate the appearance of biting mosquitoes: the floodplain species that often cause significant nuisance along rivers are barely to be seen this season, whereas invasive species are increasingly present in residential areas, particularly Asian tiger mosquitoes, the OKF said. In a statement on Monday, the directorate noted that tiger mosquito larvae can develop in large numbers in as little as a glassful of water, so after rain or garden watering numerous ideal breeding sites spring up around homes, MTI wrote.

An Aedes albopictus (Asian tiger mosquito) female mosquito obtaining a blood meal from a human host. Source: Wikimedia Commons/James Gathany/CDC

Where native larvae still survive

For the larvae of Hungary’s native mosquitoes, suitable habitat has all but disappeared, with the exception of the Tisza Lake area, where fluctuating water levels create favourable conditions for development. There, on stretches not covered by nature conservation protection, specialists are carrying out both biological larviciding and treatments targeting adult mosquitoes.

Limits of organised control over invasives

The breeding sites of invasive mosquitoes lie beyond the reach of organised intervention, since the overwhelming majority form on private property. Where their numbers become overwhelming, treatments are conducted after sunset, in the late evening and night hours, using spraying equipment mounted on flatbed vehicles, officials said.

Where spraying vehicles will appear

In the coming days, mosquito-control vehicles can be expected in several settlements in Baranya, Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén and Békés counties, with targeted partial treatments planned in one district of Budapest and in certain neighbourhoods of Szeged. A detailed list of affected settlements with planned control dates is available on the disaster management website, while residents can also follow updates on the official media channels of the relevant local councils.

World.title: Free events across Budapest on 20 August, including in the Buda Castle District and at the Citadella
World.content:
On August 20, the feast of Hungary’s foundation, the St Stephen’s Hall and its associated exhibition in the Buda Castle District, as well as the Bastion of Liberty exhibition at the Citadella, will be open free of charge, though advance registration is required. The evening fireworks display will be visible from several vantage points across the Buda Castle District and the Citadella, but given the expected heavy demand and holiday traffic restrictions, visitors are advised to plan their arrival in advance; closures and capacity limits are likely at certain locations.

The magnificent St Stephen’s Hall and the Citadella on the Gellért Hill

The reborn marvel of Buda Castle, St Stephen’s Hall, is open free of charge on August 20. Pre-registration for entry was available via szentistvanterem.hu, but owing to overwhelming interest, free slots were quickly exhausted. Nevertheless, on the day itself a limited number of on-site registrations will still be accepted. The same registration also grants free access to The Hauszmann Story exhibition, likewise housed within Buda Castle.

The Citadella’s spring opening, The Bastion of Liberty exhibition, is also free to visitors; advance booking can be made at citadella.hu. From 3pm, the Citadella’s inner park will host free family and musical programmes.

Glass bridge and renovated interior of the gun tower at the Citadel. Photo: Facebook / National Hauszmann Programme

Getting around and viewing the fireworks

As both the Buda Castle District and the Citadella offer views of the evening fireworks from various points, it is wise to check pedestrian access in advance.During the day, the Buda Castle District will be accessible via public transport to Dísz tér, approached through Szent György tér. On foot, visitors can walk up from Clark Ádám tér along the Ellyps promenade or via Palota út, though longer queues should be expected at the Tabán lifts leading from Palota út to Csikós udvar.

Between 6pm and 10pm, the Buda Castle District will no longer be accessible from the direction of Várkert Bazár; the Várkert Bazár Öntőház courtyard and the Vízhordó steps will also be closed to through traffic. After 10pm, however, it will again be possible to descend from the Buda Castle District towards Várkert Bazár: from Savoyai terrace via the Keleti access road and the Vízhordó steps, or by using the Mária lift.

The fireworks can be followed from several points in the Buda Castle District, including Savoyai terrace, the Halászó gyerekek (Fishing Children) terrace, the section of Szent György tér between the Buda Castle Funicular and the Habsburg Gate (where the wooden panoramic steps will, however, be closed), and parts of the Várkert Bazár’s Neo-Renaissance garden.

The Citadella is reachable on foot from Erzsébet bridge and Szent Gellért tér via the Gellért Hill footpaths, as well as from the Búsuló Juhász stop (served by public transport) along Szirtes út. During the fireworks, for security reasons only a limited number of visitors will be permitted on the northern viewpoints within the fortress walls; entry will be on a first-come, first-served basis. There will be no capacity limits on the promenade encircling the Citadella outside the fortress walls, nor on the terrace around the Liberty Statue, though the fireworks will be fully visible only from certain points there.

If you missed: Over 1,000-year-old authentic image of Saint Stephen, Hungary’s founder, on an unexpected relic

Organisers caution that, according to press reports, this year’s display will be concentrated primarily over the Danube stretch between the Chain Bridge and Margit Bridge; consequently, the full programme may not be clearly visible from every point in the Buda Castle District and the Citadella. In view of the expected high temperatures, visitors are urged to bring sufficient fluids; free water stations will, however, be available in both the Buda Castle District and at the Citadella.

Ten further free events across Budapest

1. Anniversary audio-visual show and shorter fireworks display

Location: Danube between the Chain Bridge and Margit Bridge

Time: Evening of August 20

Why it is worth it: This year’s headline act breaks with tradition: the classic fireworks, shorter than usual at just ten minutes, will be accompanied by a monumental visual show above the Danube, featuring light projections and drones.

2. Dance floor and light show in front of Parliament

Location: Kossuth tér

Time: Late evening, August 20

Why it is worth it: Immediately after the light show, Kossuth tér will be transformed into a vast open-air dance floor. The illuminated Parliament building will provide a striking backdrop to the night’s most irresistible beats at this free, open-air party.

Concert on the Kossuth Square near the Hungarian Parliament on 9 May. Photo: Facebook/Presser Gábor

3. Free museum entry at state institutions

Location: Various Budapest museums

Time: All day, August 20

Why it is worth it: An excellent alternative for those seeking to avoid the crowds: on the national holiday, the permanent exhibitions of most state-run museums can be visited entirely free of charge, with no admission ticket required.

Kurultáj 2026: Three days when Hungary’s Great Plain returned to the age of the steppe – Photo gallery

4. Hungarian Defence Forces’ traditional air parade on the national holiday

Location: Airspace above the Danube (Pest and Buda lower and upper embankments)

Time: Morning of August 20

Why it is worth it: Aerial demonstrations, roaring fighter jets and helicopter formations will slice across the Budapest sky, visible along the full length of the river embankments.

5. St Stephen’s Day state ceremony and oath-taking

Location: Kossuth tér

Time: Morning, August 20

Why it is worth it: The official state ceremony begins with the military honour guard’s procession of the Hungarian flag, followed by the solemn oath of defence officer cadets.

6. Open Carmelite Monastery and free castle visit

Location: Buda Castle, Carmelite Monastery

Time: August 20, 8am–4pm

Why it is worth it: On this day, doors normally kept closed will be opened: visitors will be able to walk freely into the Carmelite Monastery building and its surroundings at no charge.

7. Elektro Rakpart – electronic music festival

Location: Műegyetem rakpart

Time: August 19–20

Why it is worth it: For those seeking festival atmosphere rather than a more sedate celebration, international and Hungarian electronic music heavyweights such as Nina Kraviz and Carl Craig will be spinning hits free of charge along the Műegyetem embankment.

8. Festival and panorama at the Citadella

Location: Citadella

Time: From 3pm on August 20 until the evening fireworks

Why it is worth it: At the “roof of Budapest”, visitors can expect a picnic atmosphere, acoustic concerts (including the Pepita band) and sweeping views for those waiting out the evening lights from Gellért Hill.

9. Military hardware up close in City Park

Location: Városliget (City Park)

Time: August 20, 10am–6pm

Why it is worth it: A distinctly family-friendly, interactive event offering the chance to examine the latest military vehicles, weapons and defence equipment at close quarters.

10. Holy Right procession

Location: Szent István tér (St Stephen’s Basilica)

Time: August 20, 6pm–8pm

Why it is worth it: The most important and defining sacred event of the holiday, reviving deep cultural and historical traditions in the heart of the city centre.

World.title: Indonesian Independence Day in Budapest: why 17 August matters
World.content:
The Independence Day of the Republic of Indonesia in Budapest, which falls on 17 August, takes special significance as Indonesians in Hungary commemorate 81 years since the proclamation of Indonesia’s independence. At the Embassy of Indonesia in Budapest, independence day will be marked by the raising of Indonesia’s red-and-white national flag, the Merah Putih alongside traditions familiar to all Indonesians.

17 August marks the moment in 1945 when Indonesia proclaimed its independence following a long period of Dutch colonization and more than three years of Japanese occupation during the Second World War. More than eight decades later, the anniversary remains the most important national day celebrated in Indonesia and by Indonesians overseas.

The importance of 17 August

Indonesia’s independence was proclaimed in Jakarta on 17 August 1945, by Soekarno and Mohammad Hatta, who would become the country’s first president and vice-president. This came two days after Japan surrendered at the end of the Second World War. The brief declaration put forward a significant principle behind it: Indonesia was asserting its own independence rather than waiting for it to be granted by a colonial power.

Photo: Embassy of the Republic of Indonesia in Budapest

This was also expressed in the opening of Indonesia’s 1945 Constitution, providing that independence is the right of all nations and that colonialism must therefore be abolished. This was also during a time when the right of colonised peoples to independence has not been recognised under international law. However, the proclamation did not immediately end the conflict and the struggle for sovereignty continued, as the Netherlands attempted to restore control after the Second World War.

Following four years of armed struggle, diplomacy and negotiations, the Netherlands transferred sovereignty in December 1949. For Indonesia, however, independence did not begin with that transfer. The republic considered itself independent from the moment independence was proclaimed on 17 August 1945. Today, Independence Day commemorates the birth of the republic and also the sacrifices made during the struggle to establish independence.

Photo: Embassy of the Republic of Indonesia in Budapest

Indonesia would later become an active advocate of decolonisation and self-determination. In 1955, it hosted the Asian-African Conference in Bandung, bringing together countries from Asia and Africa against the wider backdrop of colonialism and the emerging post-war international order.

Today, Indonesia is the world’s largest archipelagic country and one of the most populous nations. Its enormous geographic and cultural diversity means that national symbols and Independence Day traditions play an important role in creating a shared sense of identity across thousands of islands and hundreds of ethnic communities.

Photo: Embassy of the Republic of Indonesia in Budapest

This is also reflected in Indonesia’s national motto, Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, translated as “Unity in Diversity”. For Indonesians living overseas, that symbolism can become even stronger.

Indonesian Independence Day in Budapest centres on the flag ceremony

The Indonesian Independence Day ceremony in Budapest is conducted at the Embassy of the Republic of Indonesia on 17 August, bringing together members of the Indonesian community living across Hungary. One of the central elements is the raising of Indonesia’s red-and-white national flag, the Merah Putih.

Ahead of the event, young Indonesians in Hungary were invited to volunteer for the Paskibra, the ceremonial flag-hoisting team. After a selection process, three participants were chosen to specifically raise the flag.

Photo: Embassy of the Republic of Indonesia in Budapest

The role carries symbolic importance during Independence Day celebrations in Indonesia, where flag ceremonies are held at schools, government institutions, communities and public spaces across the country.

In Budapest, the ceremony also serves to pass the traditions associated with the national day to younger Indonesians living thousands of kilometres from their ancestral home.

Traditional outfits as a reflection of diversity

Participants in Budapest are also using the occasion to display Indonesia’s cultural diversity, with officials wearing traditional outfits associated with different regions of the country, while guests have been encouraged to attend in traditional outfits.

This reflects the principle of Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, bringing Indonesia’s different regional and cultural identities together on a national occasion.

Indonesia’s Kartini and Hungary’s Blanka Teleki: how women shaped nations

One of the most famous outfits, Batik is Indonesia’s best-known textile traditions, and has become particularly closely associated with Indonesian identity both at home and abroad.

For an international audience in Hungary, the Budapest ceremony offers a glimpse of the variety of traditions that exist within Indonesia.

Tumpeng brings independence celebrations to the table

Following the flag ceremony, the community marks the anniversary with a traditional tumpengan. Where nasi tumpeng, a cone-shaped mound of yellow rice served with a variety of side dishes.

Tumpeng is commonly associated with important celebrations, thanksgiving and communal gatherings in Indonesia. The ceremonial cutting and sharing of the dish gives the Independence Day event a more communal dimension after the formal flag-raising.

For members of the diaspora, familiar food can also provide a direct connection to home and sharing tumpeng also provides a connection to traditions associated with national celebrations.

Beyond Bali: 10 Indonesian Destinations Perfect for Your Summer Escape

Celebrations continue beyond 17 August

The Indonesian community’s celebrations in Hungary extend beyond 17 August. On 22 August, a Pesta Rakyat, or People’s Festival, is planned with Indonesian traditional dance and musical performances prepared by members of the community.

Together, the events show how national traditions can take on new meaning abroad. For Indonesians in Hungary, commemorating 17 August connects the community not only with the traditions of Independence Day, but also with the historical significance of the date itself.

Eighty-one years after the proclamation, 17 August continues to mark Indonesia’s assertion that independence belonged to its people as a right. When the Merah Putih is raised in Budapest, it recalls the same declaration made in Jakarta in 1945.

World.title: Kurultáj 2026: Three days when Hungary’s Great Plain returned to the age of the steppe – Photo gallery
World.content:
Horsemen, warriors, yurts, falconers, archers and delegations from across the Turkic world transformed the plains of Bugac for three days. Kurultáj, one of Hungary’s most spectacular traditional heritage events, returned between 14 and 16 August 2026, drawing tens of thousands of visitors and turning a corner of the Great Hungarian Plain into a vast celebration of steppe cultures, historical memory and identity.

For an international visitor, Kurultáj can be difficult to fit into a single category. It is part historical re-enactment, part folk festival and part international cultural gathering. Its programme combines mounted archery and reconstructed battles with archaeological exhibitions, traditional music, crafts, academic presentations and representatives of nations and communities from Central Asia and beyond.

But the story of the Hungarian Kurultáj did not begin in Bugac.

From Kazakhstan to Hungary: the origins of Kurultáj

The word kurultai historically referred to an assembly or council among various Central Asian and steppe peoples. The contemporary Hungarian event, however, is a modern heritage festival rather than the direct continuation of a medieval institution.

Its modern history is closely associated with Hungarian anthropologist András Zsolt Bíró and research carried out among the Madjar community in Kazakhstan. A study examining Y-chromosomal similarities between the Kazakh Madjars and Hungarian populations was later published in the American Journal of Physical Anthropology.

According to the organisers’ account of the festival’s history, the first modern Kurultáj involving a Hungarian delegation was held in the Kazakh settlement of Saga in 2007. A year later, the first Hungarian event took place at Bösztörpuszta, with more than 30 historical re-enactment groups and a Kazakh delegation attending.

The gathering moved to Bugac in 2010 and expanded dramatically. That year, the organisers invited representatives not only of the Kazakh Madjar community but also of numerous peoples identifying with Hun and Turkic cultural traditions. Seventeen nations were represented, according to the festival’s official history.

Kurultaj 2026 in Bugac, Hungary, featuring traditional costumes, horsemen, historical reenactments and Hungarian cultural heritage. Source: Anadolu

Since then, Kurultáj has become inseparable from Bugac, a village and vast grassland area in Bács-Kiskun County, roughly 120 kilometres south-east of Budapest.

If you missed it – Our report from 2025: Europe’s most magnificent traditional event, drawing thousands of participants from dozens of countries: PHOTOS

Kurultáj 2026 brings tens of thousands to Bugac

This year’s three-day programme began on Friday, 14 August, before reaching its busiest point over the weekend. The official programme included horse shows, traditional music and dance, combat demonstrations, mounted archery, falconry, wrestling and other heritage sports.

The scale was particularly visible during Saturday’s grand military parade. According to local news portal BAON, tens of thousands attended the weekend programme as mounted and foot re-enactors wearing reconstructed Hun, Avar and Hungarian Conquest-period equipment entered the arena.

Kurultaj 2026 in Bugac, Hungary, featuring traditional costumes, horsemen, historical reenactments and Hungarian cultural heritage. Source: Anadolu

One of the major battle demonstrations recreated an episode from the Hungarians’ western military campaign of 926, complete with mounted archers and tactical manoeuvres inspired by early medieval steppe warfare. Falconry and scenes depicting nomadic life were also presented to the crowds.

The visual spectacle extended far beyond the arena. A large yurt village was built for the festival, while Uzbek, Turkmen, Azerbaijani and Uyghur crafts were presented in the Eastern Bazaar. Kazakh, Kyrgyz and Mongolian exhibition yurts introduced visitors to the material cultures of the participating peoples.

Archaeology and anthropology bring the past to life

Kurultaj 2026 in Bugac, Hungary, featuring traditional costumes, horsemen, historical reenactments and Hungarian cultural heritage. Source: Anadolu

Kurultaj 2026 also offers a major archaeological and anthropological programme inside the Ancestors’ Tents, a group of giant yurts created in cooperation with several museums and scientific institutions. The exhibitions explore the heritage of the Hunnic, Avar and Hungarian Conquest periods through reconstructed weapons, horse tack, jewellery, everyday objects and original anthropological finds, alongside facial reconstructions of people who lived in these eras. Visitors can also see exhibitions devoted to traditional bow-making, decorated sabretache plates associated with the Conquest-period elite, and a reconstruction based on the skull of a Pecheneg warrior.

At the centre of the exhibition area stands Atilla’s Tent, a yurt more than 20 metres in diameter. It houses archaeological displays, anthropological reconstructions and the monumental Arrival of the Huns semicircular painting, which stretches for more than 20 metres and evokes the Hunnic period in the Carpathian Basin.

Previous event – Discover Kurultaj 2024: Hungary’s grandest traditional event captured in photos

More than historical re-enactment

Kurultáj has increasingly developed an international dimension. More than 25 nations were represented by flags during the main ceremony this year, BAON reported. András Zsolt Bíró, president of the Hungarian Turan Association and chief organiser of the gathering, addressed the crowd alongside Mustafa Şahin, president of the Turkic Academy.

For Hungary, this aspect of the event is also connected to the country’s growing political and diplomatic engagement with Türkiye and Central Asia.

A report by 24.hu notes that high-ranking Turkish, Kyrgyz and Uzbek political figures have visited Bugac over the years, while Hungarian politicians have also appeared at the festival.

This mixture of heritage, politics and national identity is one reason Kurultáj has also generated debate.

Night show at Kurultáj 2026

A temporary world on the Hungarian puszta

What is beyond dispute is the scale of the cultural phenomenon Kurultáj has become. For three days, hundreds of horses, historical re-enactors, musicians, craftsmen and international guests occupy a temporary settlement of yurts and tents on the Bugac plain.

Then, almost as quickly as it appeared, the settlement disappears.

That temporary character is perhaps part of Kurultáj’s appeal. History is not displayed behind museum glass but performed in front of thousands of spectators: horses thunder across the arena, arrows fly, traditional instruments sound from the stages and visitors walk between yurts belonging to communities separated by thousands of kilometres.

Whether approached as historical re-enactment, an expression of national identity or an unusual meeting point between Hungary and the cultures of the Eurasian steppe, Kurultáj has grown in less than two decades into one of the country’s most distinctive summer gatherings – and one of its most visually striking.

World.title: Romania’s Constitutional Court upholds controversial integrity law amendment
World.content:
The Constitutional Court (CCR) ruled on Monday, August 17, that the modified law governing the National Integrity Agency (ANI) is partially constitutional, despite amendments that would apply retroactively, contrary to all legislative principles and the Romanian Constitution itself.

The law was at the center of a major debate last month, and its form was changed dramatically through amendments authored by the Social Democratic Party, or PSD. The same ANI law is a milestone in the European Commission-backed Recovery and Resilience Facility, or PNRR, with EUR 770 million in funding attached.

The most controversial amendment stipulates that elected officials in office lose their mandate within 30 days if they receive a final decision of incompatibility or conflict of interest, even if this decision predates the new law. This means that the law would apply retroactively.

Moreover, in this form, the bill would target Dominic Fritz, the leader of the center-right reformist party Union Save Romania or USR, one of the main opponents of PSD. In June, Romania's High Court of Cassation and Justice upheld a Timișoara Court of Appeal ruling that found Dominic Fritz in an administrative conflict of interest. Fritz, who has held the position of mayor of Timișoara since September 2020 and is currently serving his second term, was also banned from running for office for a period of three years from the end of his current term.

After being passed by Parliament, the modified ANI law had been contested before the Constitutional Court by more than two dozen senators from the National Liberal Party (PNL) and their allies in the Save Romania Union (USR), according to HotNews.

Before the ruling was issued, the constitutional judges requested that CCR president Simina Tănăsescu be removed from her capacity as reporting judge. She was replaced by another judge, Csaba Asztalos. The move came after a controversy surrounding Tănăsescu's meeting with interim prime minister Ilie Bolojan at the office of the president of the Senate. The discussion between Bolojan and Simina Tănăsescu took place on August 14 and sparked critical reactions both from within the justice system and from far-right opposition politicians. In addition, 16 presidents of Courts of Appeal and 50 presidents of Tribunals have requested explanations for the same meeting.

After the change, the PSD amendment was declared constitutional with the majority of votes of the 9 CCR judges. By a 5-3 majority vote, the CCR judges also declared constitutional the automatic termination of public office 30 days after the law enters into force for elected officials found definitively to be incompatible or in a conflict of interest.

On the other hand, the institution unanimously rejected amendments to the same law from the Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) party, which would have forced “the husband, wife or person who has relations similar to those between spouses” of high-ranking officials to submit asset declarations.

For the ANI law to move forward and be promulgated by president Nicușor Dan, it must be brought into line with the Court’s decision. Plenary sessions will need to be convened in the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate to remove the amendment declared unconstitutional by the CCR.

“Instead of stopping a brutal abuse of power, the PSD majority in the Constitutional Court has just validated it. If the president promulgates the ANI law, my mandate as mayor will end in 30 days, as a retroactive sanction for things that happened before the law entered into force. The need of the privileged mafia to get rid of me makes them act so desperately that they are going as far as dismantling the foundations of democracy,” Fritz said.

He also pointed to Article 15 of the Constitution, which states that “the law shall apply only for the future.” “From now on, any parliamentary majority can invent punishments for the past, tailored in the name of a political opponent, and the politically controlled Constitutional Court will endorse them,” he added.

World.title: Romanian woman raises GBP 500,000 for startup in UK
World.content:
Raluca Epureanu, a Romanian woman from Constanța active in the London hospitality market, has received GBP 500,000 in pre-seed funding for FlairMakers, the startup she founded, according to a RePatriot press release sent on Monday, August 17.

The funding was led by SFC Capital, one of the most active seed investors in the UK, alongside angel investors. The money raised will support product and technology development, as well as the expansion of the FlairMakers network in the UK. The company is already active in Romania and recently entered into a partnership with the Bucharest University of Economic Studies, Epureanu’s alma mater.

The startup helps a hotel or restaurant quickly find the right people when it needs them, while allowing professionals to turn their experience into a more flexible career and multiple sources of income. A hotel may need a chef for a busy weekend, a restaurant may need a sommelier, an event may require additional staff, and a company may temporarily need an experienced manager.

Instead of traditional recruitment or informal referral networks, FlairMakers creates a digital system in which companies can access verified independent professionals. The platform integrates verification, training, compliance, contracting, payments, and quality control.

“Hospitality has always operated on the assumption that there are only two ways to work: employment or agencies. There is a third, and the best professionals in the industry are already living it: the same sommelier works shifts at three venues, holds tasting courses and provides consulting for wine lists. One set of skills, multiple sources of income,” said Raluca Epureanu.

This is the idea behind what the company calls “portfolio career,” a career in which a professional can leverage the same skill in multiple contexts, for multiple clients and through multiple sources of income.

FlairMakers is already active in both the UK and Romania, being named Hospitality, Tourism & Events StartUp of the Year at the London UK StartUp Awards 2026.

RePatriot, the Romanian Business Leaders initiative that seeks to reconnect Romania to its entrepreneur diaspora, noted in a press release that FlairMakers is a concrete example of how the diaspora can transform international experience into capital, technology, know-how and networks.

“Raluca Epureanu is a remarkable example of a generation of Romanians who should no longer be viewed through the paradigm of leaving and returning. She shows that there is something much more powerful: connection. You can leave Constanța, build an extraordinary international career, learn in the world’s major centers, and then build a global company that also operates in Romania,” said Marius Bostan, initiator of RePatriot.

Raluca Epureanu has approximately 20 years of experience in the hospitality industry, built across four continents and in 30 countries. She graduated from the Bucharest University of Economic Studies, then completed an Executive MBA at Saïd Business School, University of Oxford, becoming the first Romanian woman to receive a Forté scholarship for women as part of an EMBA program. In 2022, she was included by Poets & Quants in the “The Best & Brightest Executive MBAs” ranking.

For more than 15 years, Raluca worked for Marriott International, where she progressed from an internship in the United States to the position of Senior Director of Events for the Asia-Pacific region, based in Hong Kong. In this role, she coordinated an organization covering 750 hotels, 23 brands in 24 countries, and a team of 175,000 people. In 2023, Raluca Epureanu was included in the Top 100 Romanians Abroad, the RePatriot initiative that annually recognizes the achievements of Romanian professionals and entrepreneurs in the diaspora.

World.title: Romania promoted as tourist destination at BBC Proms for first time
World.content:
Romania is being promoted as a cultural and tourist destination throughout the 2026 BBC Proms, marking the country’s first tourism campaign at the classical music festival. A page titled “Discover Romania” appears in the official brochure accompanying each of this year’s 63 concerts.

The campaign is supported by Romania’s Ministry of Economy, Digitalization, Entrepreneurship, and Tourism, with the involvement of the Romanian Cultural Institute (ICR) in London.

Founded in 1895, the BBC Proms opened its 2026 edition on July 17. Romania’s first promotional campaign at the festival coincided with pianist Alexandra Dariescu’s BBC Proms debut.

Dariescu performed at London’s Royal Albert Hall on August 5 alongside Manchester’s Hallé Orchestra, conducted by Kahchun Wong. She played Nadia Boulanger’s Fantasy for Piano and Orchestra, which was also performed at the festival for the first time.

According to ICR London, Alexandra Dariescu is the first Romanian female pianist invited to perform on the Royal Albert Hall stage during the BBC Proms. The official brochure for her concert also included a page dedicated to Romanian cultural diplomacy in the United Kingdom and the activity of ICR London.

“It is both a joy and a responsibility to make Romania’s beauty known abroad,” said Alin Grigore, director general of the Tourism Directorate within the Ministry of Economy, Digitalization, Entrepreneurship, and Tourism.

“We have extraordinary stories to tell through our culture, our people, our heritage, and the places that make us unique. Our presence at BBC Proms is an opportunity to take this message further and inspire an international audience to discover Romania, turning it into a destination they want to visit,” he added.

Alin Grigore further said that promoting Romania means showing international audiences the country’s authenticity and the people who make it special.

“We are extremely pleased with this double first: Alexandra Dariescu’s highly successful BBC Proms debut and the promotion of Romania as a cultural and tourist destination at this prestigious festival,” stated, in turn, Aura Woodward, director of the Romanian Cultural Institute in London.

World.title: Four historic estates in Romania to host outdoor film, music and poetry weekends in September
World.content:
Four historic estates in Romania will host European film screenings, live music, contemporary poetry, and cultural activities during four consecutive weekends next month. Organized by the Metropolis Cultural Association in partnership with the Pro Patrimonio Foundation, the first Film la Conac - Curți Deschise will run from September 4 to 27.

Each location will host a three-day program featuring outdoor screenings of recent European films, acoustic and contemporary concerts, poetry and sound performances, activities for children and young people, and guided tours where access conditions permit.

The circuit will begin at Neamțu Manor in Olari, Olt county, from September 4 to 6, before moving to Golescu Villa in Câmpulung Muscel, Argeș county, from September 11 to 13.

Next, Petre P. Carp Manor in Țibănești, Iași county, will host the program from September 18 to 20, while the final weekend will take place at Miclescu Manor in Călinești, Botoșani county, from September 25 to 27.

A large screen will be installed in the courtyard of each estate for three evenings of open-air cinema. The selection focuses on recent European auteur productions with internationally recognized filmmaking, accessible stories, humor, emotion, and strong visual elements, according to the organizers.

Films included in the first edition’s selection are Ildikó Enyedi’s Silent Friend, Little Amélie, Richard Linklater’s Nouvelle Vague, and Paolo Sorrentino’s La Grazia. The program aims to introduce contemporary European cinema to audiences who do not regularly attend film festivals or arthouse cinemas.

Meanwhile, the music program will feature artists working at the intersection of tradition and contemporary styles, with performances adapted to the intimate setting of the historic courtyards, the organizers also said. Invited musicians include Simona Delegeanu and Sara Eslami, while further acts will be announced alongside the complete schedules for the four weekends.

The literary component will present contemporary poetry through voice, rhythm, music, and sound rather than conventional readings. Participating writers include Moni Stănilă, Ligia Keșișian, Marius Aldea, Sorin Despot, and Ioana Tătărușanu.

Children and teenagers will be able to join stop-motion animation and creative writing workshops, as well as heritage treasure hunts inspired by the architecture and history of each site. Pro Patrimonio will also organize guided tours presenting the history, transformations, and conservation work associated with the estates where access is possible.

Moreover, Film la Conac will also include an information and fundraising campaign for the Perticari-Davila Manor in Izvoru, Argeș county. The estate became the property of the Pro Patrimonio Foundation in 2025, and its immediate needs include safety works and studies required before restoration can begin.

Visitors attending the four weekends will be able to learn about the estate and contribute to its preservation through the foundation’s official donation channel.

World.title: Body found in Romania believed to be British teen missing since November 2025
World.content:
The body of 18-year-old British citizen George Smyth, a geology student at the University of Bristol, was found during search operations in Romania, according to an announcement from the Avon and Somerset Police cited by The Guardian.

Smyth went missing in November 2025. The student, originally from Newport, Shropshire, is believed to have left Poiana Brașov heading towards Bran. He reached the Țigănești area, from where he made an emergency call for help due to extreme exhaustion. A full-scale rescue operation was launched to find the missing teenager. Canine teams also took part in the search-and-rescue operation, while drones and helicopters were used.

Sebastian Marinescu, from the local Salvamont service, had previously told the BBC that the 18-year-old “was disoriented, physically exhausted and already showing signs of hypothermia” when rescuers received the emergency call.

Rescuers said that the young man was in a “very isolated and difficult-to-access mountainous area.” At the same time, weather conditions were extremely severe, with strong winds, heavy snowfall and dense fog. As a result, the operation had to be ended.

On Wednesday, August 12, mountain rescue teams announced that they had resumed searches in “the previously indicated areas, beneath the rock walls, in hard-to-access sectors,” but without success, according to Libertatea.

However, on Friday, August 14, parts of a human skeleton were discovered by two shepherds. Salvamont rescuers had searched the area recently, but the exact location where the body was found was covered in ice. A day later, Smyth’s family was informed that a body with his identification documents was found.

“We are all devastated by George’s death. He was the best of us and is deeply missed by his younger brothers, family and friends,” they said, according to the same source. “We want to thank Salvamont mountain rescue, who have worked tirelessly since November searching for George, despite very difficult and often dangerous conditions,” the message read.

Following official identification, the necessary steps will be taken to repatriate Smyth’s body to the United Kingdom.

World.title: Nine Moldovan citizens investigated for stealing paintings worth EUR 9 mln in Italy
World.content:
Nine citizens of the Republic of Moldova are currently under investigation in Italy in connection with the theft of three paintings signed by Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse.

The paintings were stolen on the night of March 22 to 23 from the Fondazione Magnani Rocca museum in Mamiano di Traversetolo, near Parma.

The paintings are “Tasse et plat de cerises” (“Cup and Saucer with Cherries”), by Paul Cézanne, “Les Poissons” (“The Fish”), by Pierre-Auguste Renoir, and “Odalisque sur la terrasse” (“Odalisque on the Terrace”), by Henri Matisse. The total value of the works is estimated at more than EUR 9 million.

The three paintings were found in the possession of one of the suspects during searches ordered by prosecutors in Parma province and neighboring provinces, according to Jurnal.md.

Italian judges decided to detain five of the suspects. According to the international press, the men are believed to be part of an organized crime group suspected of committing several thefts from homes, commercial spaces and other properties. During the searches, law enforcement officers also recovered stolen goods worth tens of thousands of euros.

World.title: SVN analysis: Around 4,000 apartments under construction in Bucharest’s Aviației area
World.content:
Approximately 4,000 apartments are currently under construction in Bucharest’s Aviației area and are scheduled for completion between 2026 and 2028, according to an analysis by real estate consultancy SVN Romania. The average selling price for new apartments under development in the area stands at EUR 3,230 per usable square meter, excluding VAT.

SVN said Aviației is the capital’s main development hub for middle-market residential projects and a top destination for buyers seeking homes near the Aviației-Barbu Vǎcǎrescu business district. Projects in the area generally target the upper end of the middle-market segment and buyers with above-average incomes.

The starting price of a new one-bedroom apartment under construction averages EUR 158,000 plus VAT, while a new two-bedroom apartment starts at approximately EUR 214,000 plus VAT. Prices increase depending on the size of the property.

A household seeking to purchase a new one-bedroom apartment in the area with a mortgage would need an average monthly income of approximately RON 15,000, according to SVN’s calculations. The estimate was based on a 30-year mortgage with a fixed interest rate for the first three years, and a 25% down payment.

Meanwhile, the minimum monthly income needed to purchase a new two-bedroom apartment through a mortgage would be approximately RON 22,300. By comparison, a couple earning two average salaries in Bucharest had a combined monthly income of RON 14,620, or about EUR 2,800, based on National Institute of Statistics data for May 2026.

“The northern area of Bucharest — and, implicitly, Aviației — has always been a desirable location for prospective buyers, and those who have purchased a home here, whether in the 1980s, the 1990s or after 2020, have consistently had above-average incomes, without necessarily being luxury buyers. The current average price of a new home under development in the Aviației area is around 40% higher than the city average, a level explained by the neighborhood’s good image and by its location in the heart of Bucharest’s most important business area,” said Raluca Dobrisan, managing partner at SVN Romania Residentialist Floreasca.

Based on the number of homes sold annually in Bucharest, the residential projects under development in Aviației target approximately 4% of active buyers in the capital’s housing market.

SVN data also indicated that more than 7,200 additional homes could be developed in the area over the medium and long term, considering the land plots owned by investors active in the residential sector.

According to SVN, the analysis did not include residential projects in the Fabrica de Glucozǎ area or those located in Ilfov County.

The number of houses and apartments sold in the Bucharest–Ilfov region during the first six months of 2026 was 1.4% lower than in the same period last year. At the national level, residential sales declined by nearly 9% year-on-year, according to data from the National Agency for Cadastre and Land Registration.

World.title: Flow of Danube in Romania three times lower than multiannual August average
World.content:
The flow of the Danube, the second-longest river in Europe, will continue to decrease until the end of next week in the Romanian section. The river's volume will be three times lower than the multiannual average for August, according to the forecast issued by the National Institute of Hydrology and Water Management for the period August 15-22, 2026.

Specifically, the flow of the water in the Baziaș section, which marks the Danube’s entrance in Romania, will decrease from 1,400 cubic meters per second to 1,300, much lower than the multiannual average for August of 3,900 cubic meters per second, according to the same source, cited by Agerpres.

In the quarterly forecast, hydrologists estimated a maximum Danube flow of 2,000 cubic meters per second and a minimum of 1,450 cubic meters per second for August. Downstream from Romania’s Iron Gates, the boundary between Serbia to the south and Romania to the north, flows will generally remain stationary, with a slight downward trend.

As for the inland rivers, daily average flows will remain relatively stationary throughout August 16–22. In the second part of the period, isolated increases in water levels and flows are possible on some small rivers in hilly and mountainous areas, with a higher probability in the north, west and northwest of the country, as a result of the forecast precipitation, in the form of showers.

Last week, Romania’s nuclear group Nuclearelectrica (BVB: SNN) announced the controlled shutdown of its second nuclear reactor due to low Danube flow. The river water is paramount for the cooling process of the reactor. The energy group’s other reactor, Unit 1, had been shut down at the end of July for the same reason.

The two units together provide nearly 20% of the national electricity consumption from the grid and are the largest generating units in Romania, with 680 MW each. No date has been announced for restarting, as it all depends on the flow of the Danube.

In the meantime, Romania is forced to import energy to compensate for the loss of power, especially in the evenings.

World.title: Courting Trump’s Allies, Bosnian Croat Political Party Signs US Lobbying Contract
World.content:
For political analyst Tanja Topic from Banja Luka, it is obvious that Covic listened to his political ally Dodik and followed in his lobbying footsteps. According to her, Dodik’s experience is valuable, and every opportunity to capitalise on American support for Christian values is being used.

“Of course, the work of lobbying firms should not be equated with the positions of the State Department, nor should we blindly believe domestic spin masters who equate these activities with ‘friendship with Trump’,” Topic said. “The purpose of these activities is to lobby for the ‘Croatian issue in Bosnia and Herzegovina’, which implicitly points to a connection with the elections, while the second part concerns the biggest current US interest in BiH – the Southern Interconnection.”

Adnan Huskic, a professor of political science and international relations at the Sarajevo School of Science and Technology (SSST), previously told BIRN that this move by HDZ BiH is logical.

“It is clear that everyone has seen that American power is for sale,” Huskic said. “So they are doing this to increase their standing and their chances for any future plans.”

Karcic says that what Covic wants from Mercury Public Affairs – crisis communications and public affairs experts who can navigate the corridors of Capitol Hill – is to promote the following argument: “We are not against American gas, we are for American gas, but we want it to be managed by an organisation based in Mostar in order to ensure institutional equality.”

According to the signed contract, Mercury Public Affairs is also committed to strengthening the HDZ BiH’s relations with institutions and representatives of the United States, NATO, the European Union and “other relevant international stakeholders”.

For Karcic, in the language of lobbying in Washington, this is a classic “pro-Western shield”.

Karcic noted that the inclusion of a commitment to NATO, the US and the EU creates the impression for American decision-makers that the HDZ BiH is a stable Euro-Atlantic partner. He said this is crucial for the party because it neutralises accusations that its tactical partnership with Dodik’s Serb nationalist party SNSD is weakening the country’s pro-Western course.

“This is an attempt to brand the HDZ in Washington as a bulwark of Western values in Bosnia and Herzegovina, conveying the message that internal stability – as they see it, through Dayton and the constituent peoples [Bosniaks, Croats and Serbs] – is actually a prerequisite for the overall security architecture of this region,” Karcic said.

Bassuener considers the contract fairly standard and noted that it contains reference to the “equality of constituent peoples” and the “preservation of peace, stability, territorial integrity and the multi-ethnic character [of Bosnia and Herzegovina]“, as well as a target of presenting the HDZ BiH’s positions to the US government, elected representatives, the media and the wider public.

“However, it is considerably less explicit than statements already publicly available regarding a third entity, the ‘discrimination’ against Croats, electoral reform and similar issues,” Bassuener said.
