In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: Judges vs ordinary pensioners in Azerbaijan: what the law and figures show
World.content:
Judges and pensions in Azerbaijan

The pension of Azerbaijani judge Jahangir Yusifov was increased from 4,700 manat (around $2,765) to 7,500 manat (around $4,412) after he took the matter to court. Thanks to special pension rules, judges’ pensions can be dozens of times higher than the country’s average pension.

For comparison: the minimum labour pension in Azerbaijan is 320 manat (around $188).

When Baku Court of Appeal judge Jahangir Yusifov retired in 2025 at the age of 65, the State Social Protection Fund awarded him a monthly pension of 4,700 manat. That amount was equivalent to around 58% of his average monthly salary while serving as a judge.

Yusifov demanded that his pension be increased to 8,200 manat (around $4,824), arguing that he had worked all his life under difficult conditions, possessed special professional qualifications, and had been subject to a high level of responsibility.

The Baku Administrative Court upheld most of his claim, increasing his pension to around 7,500 manat. His request for additional financial assistance equal to 10% of his pension was rejected.

This is not the first such case. Other retired judges have filed similar claims, including Azad Majidov, Anvar Seyidov, Ulvi Mayilov and others. The courts have upheld all of the claims filed.

These cases clearly demonstrate how the special social protection mechanism provided for judges under Azerbaijani law is applied in practice.

Judges’ pension provisions

Under Article 109 of the Law “On Courts and Judges,” judges’ pensions are calculated according to special rules and depend on their length of service as a judge.

For those who have served as a judge for at least five years, the pension may be set at 45% of their average salary.

For between 5 and 10 years of service, an additional 2% is added to the 45% for each additional year.

For between 10 and 15 years of service, the pension is set at 55% of the average salary, plus 5% for each additional year, but cannot exceed 80% of the average salary.

Pension calculations also take into account pension capital and other allowances предусмотренные by law.

These higher percentage rates and additional benefits based on length of service provide judges with special pension conditions compared with other groups of the population.

Is it possible to live on a pension?

A judge’s pension of 7,500 manat (around $4,412) is 23 times higher than the minimum pension and 12–13 times higher than the average pension.

For comparison, the official subsistence minimum for a pensioner, regardless of profession, is 245 manat (around $145).

The average pension is significantly higher than this threshold. Nevertheless, it can be difficult for a single pensioner to maintain a stable standard of living solely on an average pension. Older people often need additional sources of income, such as employment, family support or targeted social assistance.

According to official statistics, as of April 1, 2026, more than 105,000 old-age pension recipients were still working.

But state officials, prosecutors and judges are provided with a fundamentally different level of social protection. Many people in Azerbaijan view this approach as a “double standard” enshrined in law. And when it comes to lawsuits filed by judges seeking higher pensions, public discussions often include comments along the lines of: “Apparently, even that wasn’t enough for the judges.”

News in Azerbaijan

World.title: Heavy rain floods streets, basements and metro stations in Tbilisi – video
World.content:
Heavy rain in Tbilisi

Following heavy rainfall overnight on 14 August, the Georgian capital was once again flooded. Tbilisi City Hall issued a statement on the situation, saying the intense rainfall had “caused certain problems”.

According to the city authorities, central districts were the worst affected. Private homes and basements were flooded, while a retaining wall at one residential property collapsed. Streets across the city and areas around several metro stations were also inundated.

Throughout the night, residents posted videos from different parts of the capital showing flooded streets and squares. Residents of one street in the city centre also blocked the road, calling for help in dealing with the damage.

Videos published by city residents:

“The heavy rainfall in the capital caused problems in all ten districts. Gravel and stones were washed onto roads. Our staff are carrying out clean-up work around the clock. The rain was particularly heavy in the Vake, Mtatsminda and Krtsanisi districts.

“More than 500 personnel and 30 pieces of equipment have been mobilised across all affected areas and are involved in the clean-up operation. The work will continue until all the problems have been fully resolved,” said Giorgi Papava, head of Tbilisi’s main municipal services operator, Tbilservice Group.

World.title: More than 32,000 applications for Armenian citizenship in a year: who is applying and why
World.content:
Rise in applications for Armenian citizenship

“There has been a sharp increase in the number of applications for Armenian citizenship. In 2025, the number exceeded 32,000, a historic high for the entire history of the Republic of Armenia,” said Armen Kazaryan, acting deputy interior minister.

According to him, the number of citizenship applications exceeded 20,000 in each of the previous two years, compared with 7,000-8,000 in earlier years.

Kazaryan believes the main goal of applicants is to obtain a document that allows them to travel:

“We have seen certain developments, in particular the outbreak of hostilities in Ukraine and restrictions on travel for Russian citizens. After that, we saw an increase in applications for Armenian citizenship. By the way, most Russian citizens applying for Armenian citizenship are ethnic Armenians.”

He rejected claims that obtaining Armenian citizenship is a complicated process:

“The requirements for ethnic Armenians are ‘zero’. People may face administrative difficulties. For example, some may lack the necessary documents proving their ethnicity, or their records may contain errors. In such cases, we need to compare the information with other records and verify it. Essentially, Armenia imposes no requirements on ethnic Armenians.”

Kazaryan himself considers the lack of requirements for ethnic Armenians problematic. In his view, this devalues the institution of citizenship itself.

“We will soon present a draft of the relevant legislative amendments addressing these issues,” he said, without specifying what changes the amendments would introduce.

Border crossings: more people entered than left

Nelli Davtyan, acting head of the Migration and Citizenship Service, also spoke to journalists. She recalled that last year Armenia recorded a “significant positive figure” in the difference between the number of citizens entering and leaving the country. The figure stood at 8,660.

In the first half of this year, the difference between entries and exits stood at 1,347.

“There were 871,409 entries and 870,062 exits. If we compare this with figures for the first half of previous years, last year’s figure was -20,065, while in 2024 it was -22,893,” Davtyan noted.

She stressed that the figure usually rises in the second half of the year. This happens because seasonal migrant workers return home after leaving the country for temporary work. They usually leave in early spring and return in autumn. Davtyan therefore described a positive figure already in the first half of the year as “exceptional”.

More than 6,000 people granted temporary residence permits

Armen Kazaryan said Armenia had transformed from a country that “sends” migrants abroad into a country that receives migrants. “The second major trend is the growing interest in Armenia among foreign nationals,” he noted.

Nelli Davtyan said the Migration and Citizenship Service had received 9,534 applications for one-year temporary residence permits: “Of these, 6,059 were approved. Compared with previous years, the number of applications has almost tripled. The proportion of approved applications has also nearly tripled.”

According to Davtyan, the number of applications for three-year residence permits has also increased, although more modestly: “In previous years, the figure stood at 1,500-1,700, while in the first half of this year it had already reached 2,085.”

Armenia implementing 53 EU recommendations on visa liberalisation

Armen Kazaryan said Armenia was actively cooperating with the European Union on visa liberalisation. He recalled that Armenia received its first report on the implementation of the action plan in May 2026. The report gave a fairly positive assessment of the steps taken by the Armenian government.

“The EU presented us with 53 recommendations. To complete our work, we divided them into specific actions. We broke down the recommendations so that we could clearly identify the steps we need to take to implement them,” Kazaryan explained.

Based on the 53 recommendations, an Armenian working group drew up a list of 117 actions. More than half of them have already been completed.

The recommendations form part of the first stage of the visa liberalisation action plan. This stage covers legislation and policy development only. The authorities expect to assess how effectively Armenia has implemented the first stage by early 2027 or during the first half of the year. If the results prove positive, work on the second stage will begin.

World.title: Kushner talks with Hamas and Israel end without Gaza deal
World.content:
Donald Trump's envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner has wrapped up two days of meetings with Israeli and Hamas leaders to break a stalemate over the US president's Gaza plan, but there were no signs of an imminent breakthrough as both sides dug in.

Mr Kushner met Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel a day after meeting Hamas' political leader in Egypt in a bid to revive the plan, which has stalled as Israel has carried out air strikes and seized more territory in Gaza despite an October ceasefire, while Hamas has refused to give up its weapons.

The US president last month announced that Hamas had agreed to lay down its arms in phases, under a 15-point roadmap put forward by his so-called Board of Peace to advance the president's plan, as Israel's military withdraws from Gaza.

Hamas said it agreed to the roadmap but implementation depended on Israel first meeting its own commitments, including halting attacks and withdrawing.

No breakthrough in Jerusalem

Mr Netanyahu, whose ruling coalition is trailing in Israeli opinion polls ahead of an October national election, earlier this month rejected the roadmap, insisting Israel would not withdraw until Hamas is completely disarmed.

An Israeli official indicated that there was no breakthrough in the meeting, saying Mr Netanyahu had made it clear the military would not withdraw from a demarcation line set out in an October ceasefire and would continue to carry out operations in Gaza as it sees necessary, including targeting those who took part in the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel that triggered the war.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has publicly rejected Donald Trump's proposed peace plan. (Truth Social: Donald Trump)

Hamas has demanded Israel adhere to the ceasefire, while both sides have disputed the sequencing of how Mr Trump's plan to end the war would be implemented. More than 1,200 Palestinians and four Israeli soldiers have been killed in Gaza since October, according to Gazan health officials and the Israeli military.

Two sources said Mr Kushner's meeting with Mr Netanyahu lasted several hours.

Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace envoy for Gaza who is widely seen as leading efforts to implement the plan, also attended the meeting, the sources told Reuters.

The Israeli official said Mr Netanyahu and Mr Kushner agreed in the meeting that the reconstruction of Gaza would not begin until Hamas was fully disarmed, including of light weapons.

Why did Israel reject Trump's Gaza plan? Israel's rejection of Donald Trump's Gaza peace plan is not a surprise. Here's why and how politics plays into it ahead of an Israeli election.

In a statement that characterized the meeting as "deep and constructive", the prime minister's office said that Israel and the Board of Peace believe that Gaza's disarmament should be "prompt and completed before any reconstruction happens".

It also said that Mr Netanyahu had agreed with the Board of Peace to establish a working group on disarmament and demilitarization, and another working group that focuses on sanitation, clean water and other public health issues in Gaza.

A Board of Peace official described the meeting as "in-depth and very productive," saying the two sides had reached an agreement on a path forward. The official did not elaborate.

Reconstruction

US and Israeli officials have previously said that reconstruction could happen in areas of Gaza under Israeli control or a new Palestinian technocratic government.

The Board of Peace has indicated that while rifles would be prohibited, some personal weapons would be permitted under Palestinian law.

The proposed plan would see Hamas agree to disarm itself in exchange for the withdrawal of Israeli forces from Gaza. (Reuters: Mahmoud Issa)

Mr Netanyahu is facing a tough reelection campaign and diplomats say it is unlikely Israel's longest-serving prime minister would make any concessions over Gaza before the October 27 vote.

Mr Kushner and Mr Mladenov were in Israel after meeting with Hamas political leader Khalil Al-Hayya in Egypt on Sunday.

It marks Mr Kushner's second known meeting with representatives of Hamas, the Palestinian militant group designated a terrorist movement by the United States.

Mr Kushner previously met Hamas officials alongside US envoy Steve Witkoff in October 2025, helping clinch a deal that led to a ceasefire in Gaza and the release of remaining hostages seized by Hamas.

Reuters

World.title: Ancient clash with 'Kraken' galaxy 12 billion years ago helped form Milky Way
World.content:
Our home galaxy the Milky Way has grown in size by crashing into its neighbours for billions of years.

One of the biggest crashes we know of, just over 10 billion years ago, was with a galaxy with the enigmatic name of "Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus".

Now, evidence is mounting that another, similarly large, galactic merger happened 2 billion years prior.

In a study published in Nature Astronomy, researchers have dubbed this merging galaxy "Low-energy-Kraken-Heracles" after a Nordic sea monster and a Greek god (we'll get into how galaxies are named later).

Lead author Davide Massari, a researcher at the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics, said the existence of the 12-billion-year-old merger had been hotly debated.

To gather more evidence about the ancient galaxy, the researchers studied the ages of tight-knit groups of stars known as "globular clusters".

The ages and chemical compositions of each cluster pointed to the galaxies they originally formed in, before they mixed with the Milky Way in a merger event.

"Finding such a clear-cut signature in the age of globular clusters made us very happy," Dr Massari said.

Galactic archaeology on clusters of stars

The Milky Way first formed about 800 million years after the big bang 13.8 billion years ago.

Back then our galaxy would have been a small disc of gas.

Today, the Milky Way is about 100,000 light years across and contains up to 400 billion stars.

Previous studies suggest most of these stars formed between 11 and 7 billion years ago.

Luca Casagrande, an astrophysicist at the Australian National University who wasn't involved with the research, said that younger galaxies seen closer to the big bang are all much smaller than our Milky Way.

"We always knew that the Milky Way had to go through several merger events to build up," Dr Casagrande said.

"The Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus is the easy one to detect. The other ones are harder and so there is always a degree of uncertainty."

The European Space Agency's Gaia satellite had helped establish the existence of the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger, according to Dr Casagrande.

In the new study, the researchers used data from the Hubble Space Telescope to study globular clusters.

Globular clusters contain tens of thousands to millions of stars. (Supplied: ESA/Hubble; NASA)

"They determined the ages very, very precisely, of these globular clusters and with that very high precision in the ages, they were able to see essentially three main groups," Dr Casagrande said.

One of these age groups is from the original Milky Way, while another age group corresponds to the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus event.

The researchers found a distinct set of globular clusters in between these two age groups, which they said was another "satellite" galaxy that was absorbed by the Milky Way.

Duncan Forbes, an astrophysicist at Swinburne University who wasn't involved in the study, said several other astronomers (including him) had previously suggested this third large galaxy existed.

The researchers suggest NGC 6535, a globular cluster 22,000 light-years away, was once part of the Low-energy-Kraken-Heracles galaxy. (Supplied: ESA/Hubble; NASA)

"The globular clusters of this satellite have distinctive ages and chemical properties," he said.

Professor Forbes said this study had "more statistical weight" than previous research.

"With more precise relative ages, Massari [and colleagues] were able to estimate when the satellite was accreted onto the infant Milky Way," he said.

"They agree with my previous work that the satellite was one of the most massive to merge with the Milky Way as it grew in mass over cosmic time."

Sausage, Kraken… Koala?

The name of Low-energy-Kraken-Heracles comes from a combination of names suggested by different research groups while the third galaxy theory was being built.

"Low-energy" refers to the low-energy orbits of the clusters, "Kraken" is a nod to the elusive Scandinavian sea monster, and "Heracles" hails from the Greek hero associated with the formation of the Milky Way.

"A few years ago, I suggested that this satellite galaxy be called 'Koala' because both are associated with low energy," Professor Forbes said.

The name mirrors Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus: an amalgam derived from the Gaia satellite, the sausage-like shape of data from early analyses, and the son of Gaia from Greek mythology.

"For these satellite galaxies there doesn't seem to be an official naming convention," Professor Forbes said.

More mergers in Milky Way's past and future

The Milky Way is not done absorbing galaxies: it's currently merging with the small Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy, a process that started some 6 billion years ago.

In the next few billion years, it may also collide with the larger Andromeda galaxy, although astronomers aren't confident this will happen.

Andromeda may not crash into the Milky Way, but another galaxy probably will A new study challenges predictions that the Milky Way will crash into the Andromeda galaxy in 5 billion years.

Dr Massari said it was "possible, but rather unlikely" that there were still undiscovered mergers in the Milky Way's past.

"I do not think there is room for another event this massive, at least in the far away past of our galaxy," he said.

Dr Casagrande said that, while the current study was "thorough", it was still possible there were more undiscovered collisions in our galaxy's past.

"I wouldn't definitely draw the line that it was three main accretion events and that was it," Dr Casagrande said.

" Based on the current data, there is no evidence for more, but we are sampling a region of the galaxy. "

Data from newer telescopes and other regions of the galaxy might yet support more mergers, Dr Casagrande said.

"As we probe more of the galaxy and we get more data, then we might be able to recover evidence for maybe even a fourth or a fifth — who knows, right?"

World.title: Trump threatens Oman as Iran vows to escalate conflict over Hormuz
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has threatened to bomb Oman if it blocks American efforts to take control of the Strait of Hormuz, as he continues to press Iran to surrender.

It comes as Iran signals it may shift to a more aggressive military stance if peace talks with the US fail to reach an outcome.

"If Oman gets in the way, we'll bomb the s*** out of them," Mr Trump told Fox News journalist Trey Yingst, referring to ongoing talks between Oman and Iran on control of the strait.

Iranian and Omani officials have been talking for weeks on future maritime navigation arrangements through the Strait of Hormuz, which Mr Trump has floated as a future US territory.

Iran's coast flanks the north side of Hormuz and Oman lies on the south.

A large portion of the world's oil shipments flow through the Strait of Hormuz. (Reuters: Benoit Tessier)

Progress towards peace talks and a resumption of oil tanker traffic through the strategic Strait of Hormuz has ground to a halt, with no sign that the warring parties are moving towards ending the conflict that the US and Israel launched on February 28.

"Iranian entities must be prepared to escalate tensions in the Strait of Hormuz and wider region, as Iran will be ready to make decisions and take action on difficult decisions," the Iranian official said, adding that Tehran would conduct a "timely and precise" military attack to break the US naval blockade if diplomacy failed.

Monday marked the day by which Iran and the United States were expected to reach a final deal under a memorandum of understanding agreed in June and aimed at ending the war.

Signed on June 17, the MoU set out a 60-day time-frame, extendable by mutual consent, by which Washington and Tehran should reach an agreement that would cover broader issues such as the fate of Iran's nuclear programme.

The MoU, which declared the immediate and permanent cessation of military operations on all fronts, quickly unravelled, however, due to a dispute over control of the Strait of Hormuz.

Speaking to reporters on Monday afternoon, local time, Mr Trump said he was not seeking an extension to the memorandum.

Iran to set deadline

Tehran said point five of the MoU gives it the right to manage the waterway, while Washington rejected that interpretation.

Hostilities resumed as Tehran began firing on vessels it said were trying to sail through the waterway on an unapproved route.

Trump vows to declare Hormuz a US territory US President Donald Trump says he will soon declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory, escalating his rhetoric over the vital waterway that carries a significant share of global oil supplies.

US President Donald Trump said on July 7 that the pact was "over". Tehran has repeatedly accused Washington of consistently violating its commitments.

"Within the short period of a few weeks set by Iran, all the agreement's provisions must be implemented by the US. This is a precondition for further negotiations with the US," the Iranian official told Reuters, adding that mediators would share Tehran's deadline with Washington and regional states.

Both Iran and the United States have stepped up rhetoric over the past week.

Mr Trump warned Americans in a speech at a rally on Friday to prepare for continued high fuel prices as a result of the war, while also saying that "after we finish defeating Iran … pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States".

Earlier on Monday, Mr Trump posted on his Truth Social platform: "The number one Goal is, and always will be, that Iran cannot have, in any way, shape, or form, a Nuclear Weapon", repeating one of his stated rationales for the war.

Reuters

World.title: At least 68 killed in Indonesia quake as aftershocks hamper rescue efforts
World.content:
The number of people killed in a powerful earthquake in eastern Indonesia has risen to 68 as rescue workers continue to search for people trapped under rubble.

Almost 13,000 people have been evacuated following the country's deadliest disaster since 2022, with many sheltering in tents outdoors or at schools and police stations afraid to return to their homes due to fears of aftershocks.

Nearly 1,600 aftershocks have been detected in the province since Saturday, when the magnitude-7.7 quake hit the Indonesian island of Flores.

One of the most prominent, a 5.6 magnitude earthquake, was recorded on Monday morning, local time, according to the country's geophysics agency.

A school has been damaged in Reo, East Nusa Tenggara province. (AP: Firdia Lisnawati)

An official at Indonesia's disaster mitigation agency, Berton SP Panjaitan, confirmed the death toll had risen to 68, up from 54, on Monday night, local time, and that more than 200 people had been injured.

More than 1,300 homes have been damaged, with nearly 250 destroyed on Flores alone, according to the National Disaster Management Agency.

Military and police officers have been deployed across the disaster zone, supported by 10 aircraft to distribute 275 tonnes of aid to the area.

But logistical challenges have slowed deliveries to some hard-hit communities, according to Abdul Muhari, deputy chief of the country's disaster management agency.

A church in Ruteng, Manggarai regency, in the East Nusa Tenggara province, has been damaged in the quake. (Reuters: Willy Kurniawan)

Indonesian Red Cross' head of disaster management Ridwan Sobri Carman said access to isolated communities had started to improve which meant they could help with evacuation efforts and providing first aid.

"Our team is also working with the local authorities in seven districts to reach communities affected by landslides," he told The World.

" At the moment, infrastructure is quite critical. "

He said while the worst of the damage had occurred in Flores, some islands close by had also been affected.

Patients are treated in a makeshift tent outside a hospital amid fears of aftershocks in Ruteng, East Nusa Tenggara province. (AP: Firdia Lisnawati)

The National Disaster Management Agency was working with federal and international agencies on the disaster response and emergency fund, according to Ridwan Sobri Carman.

"Our houses are no longer liveable, because many have collapsed and are full of cracks, so we can't go inside anymore," Mbay resident Junaidin told AFP outside a self-made tent that was sleeping about 30 people.

"We only go back home to get water, clothes, pillows, and then we… spend the nights here."

Authorities have also set up two emergency field hospitals in the worst-hit town of Ruteng to treat earthquake victims after local hospitals were damaged, with two crisis management teams overseeing a health emergency operation centre, according to the National Disaster Management Agency.

Helmi Yanati is sheltering outside her damaged house following the earthquake, in Poco village, Manggarai regency. (Reuters: Willy Kurniawan)

During Indonesia's Independence Day ceremony in Jakarta, President Prabowo Subianto asked for people to pray for those affected by disasters in East Nusa Tenggara and other parts of the country, while leading a nationwide moment of silence honouring the nation's independence heroes.

But those affected by the disaster have called on the government to do more.

"As for help from the government, there hasn't been any — no tents, no medicine, no food, no drinking water, nothing," said Junaidin, who only has one name.

"Please open your eyes, government. We are your people, we are part of you. So please look after us."

ABC/wires

World.title: Labor and Coalition close in on deal on gambling reforms
World.content:
A "one-stop shop" allowing Australians to opt out of wagering advertising online has been agreed to by Labor and the Coalition in a tentative deal to pass the federal government's gambling reforms.

The government and opposition briefed a Labor backbench committee and the Coalition shadow ministry on about 15 amendments this evening, ahead of a full caucus and party room meeting for final approval tomorrow morning.

With shadow cabinet backing the bill, it is expected to pass — however Liberal sources have told the ABC some in the party are considering crossing the floor because they believe the laws still won't be strong enough.

Communications Minister Anika Wells used a speech in parliament today, before the deal was finalised, to signal Labor was poised to move on so-called gambling inducements and online ads, after criticism its bill did not go far enough.

"It is expected that the government's reforms will respond to these concerns by introducing new restrictions on inducement-based marketing and establishing the wagering advertising opt-out register, which will provide Australians with a one-stop shop to opt out of seeing wagering advertising on online platforms," she said.

Anika Wells flagged the government's willingness to compromise earlier today. (ABC News: Joel Wilson)

In addition to TV and radio restrictions, the government's current draft bill creates a "triple lock" system that would require social media, streaming and other online platforms only show gambling ads to logged-in users verified as over 18.

The platforms would also have to give every adult the ability to opt out, a system criticised by the Greens and Coalition as too onerous for Australians who would have to do this manually for every online account.

Some of the naysayers had advocated for an opt-in system instead, but as the ABC revealed, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was not prepared to entertain such a large change.

Instead, the compromise position put forward by the Coalition was to create a single register for Australians to indicate their wish to opt out of gambling ads.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and Mr Albanese met several times to negotiate the gambling laws, which Labor is seeking to pass by the end of this week.

The Coalition will back Labor's gambling law reforms after reaching a deal with the government. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Proposed opt-out register questioned by industry

The opt-out register would be established by the Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA), with people able to request their various online accounts be blocked from viewing gambling advertising.

It is understood the plan would be for people to provide information such as their email address linked to the platform they are seeking to opt out of ads on.

The register is not expected to be in place immediately from January 1, when the broader ad restrictions are due to take effect.

Alcohol and gambling ads 'deeply embedded' in NRL and AFL Every NRL and AFL club has an alcohol sponsor this season while every NRL and five AFL clubs are sponsored by gambling companies, a new report has found.

Its principle would be similar to the existing "do not call" register, which is a secure government database where Australians can opt out of receiving unsolicited telemarketing calls.

But tonight, multiple sources in the wagering and tech industry immediately questioned how this approach would be feasible, given the complexity and breadth of online platforms.

There were also concerns raised about who would pay for the register and how.

Currently, the federal government's wagering self-exclusion register, Betstop, is funded by gambling companies, who contribute an amount effectively based on a ratio of their market share.

But one wagering source said companies did not expect to pay for the administration of a second register for advertising.

A tech industry source said an opt-out system made available to individuals was "very different" compared to requiring platforms to proactively comply with a centralised register.

Targeted restriction of inducements proposed

Rather than a broader crackdown on gambling inducements, such as bonus bet offers, amendments to the legislation are aimed at protecting vulnerable and high-spending gamblers.

It is understood this would include creating a cooling period preventing gambling companies from sending inducements to any new accounts or to people who have recently removed themselves from Betstop.

The proposed amendments are also expected to crack down on VIP account managers at wagering companies earning commissions based on their clients' spending.

The ABC reported last year that Sportsbet and Tabcorp have already stopped this practice.

Discussions are also ongoing about an independent review mechanism to assess the effectiveness of the laws in the future.

Last week, Liberal MP Simon Kennedy used a speech in parliament to back this idea.

"There should be an independent review of wherever we land after the next election, so we can do more," he said.

Senate inquiry report makes one recommendation

A report released tonight, following a short two-day inquiry into the government's gambling legislation earlier this month, recommended the bills be passed.

The single recommendation from the government-authored report was described as "not surprising, but tragic" by independent ACT senator David Pocock.

"We heard from basically everyone other than the gambling companies who said this bill does not protect children, it doesn't break the link between sport and gambling companies," he told the ABC.

Senator Pocock wrote a dissenting report from the inquiry, calling on the government to implement the original recommendations put forward in the You Win Some, You Lose More report by late Labor MP Peta Murphy.

This included a full ban on gambling ads being phased in over three years, an immediate ban on gambling inducements, and the establishment of a single national online gambling regulator.

Senator Pocock also provided fallback amendments to strengthen Labor's existing bill, including extending the gambling ad ban during live sport to after 8:30pm, and replacing the online opt-out "triple lock" system with an opt-in model.

David Pocock called on the government to adopt the recommendations of Peta Murphy's report. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

In his report, Senator Pocock referenced evidence given to the inquiry by the family of a 24-year-old man with a severe gambling addiction who died by suicide.

The witnesses told the Senate committee there were "no words to describe this pain", and the family now "lives a half-life".

The Greens also provided a dissenting report, arguing the minor party would not support the bill in its current form.

Greens communications spokeswoman senator Sarah Hanson-Young called for a complete ban on all online gambling ads, the establishment of a national regulator and an end to inducements.

She also recommended the introduction of separate legislation requiring gambling companies to forfeit money they received that was the proceeds of crime.

That was based on evidence heard by the inquiry that wagering companies could retain money gambled by customers who obtained it through criminal offending.

World.title: Fauci could face prison if convicted of contempt, former prosecutor says
World.content:
Medical experts say the persecution of Anthony Fauci is weakening America's health system and preventing the world from learning valuable lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic.

Georges Benjamin, chief executive of the American Public Health Association, says US health professionals are frightened by what has happened to Dr Fauci.

"They're afraid to do their jobs that they know need to get done because they're afraid they'll be criticised," he said.

The US Department of Justice is weighing whether to prosecute Dr Fauci over his refusal to answer the questions of a Congressional Committee.

He appeared last month under subpoena before the US Senate committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, but invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination.

Dr Fauci was given a pre-emptive pardon by former president Joe Biden in January 2025, covering all actions he took from 2014 to 2025. However, Republican senators argue that doesn't exempt him from answering their questions, and he could still face charges for anything after that date.

Anthony Fauci appearing before the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in Washington DC. (Reuters: Nathan Howard)

Former US federal prosecutor Amanda Vaughn has told 7.30 that a contempt charge against Dr Fauci was possible.

"I would not be surprised at all," Ms Vaughn said.

"There's some case law that's on Dr Fauci's side here," she said, "but we're in a little bit of a different environment, so it'll be interesting to see what the Department of Justice does."

If convicted, Ms Vaughn said it was possible Dr Fauci could be sentenced to time in prison.

Dr Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment rights more than 100 times during the Senate committee hearing.

"It was a show trial really," said Gavin Yamey, a professor at Duke University's Global Health Institute.

Donald Trump listens as Anthony Fauci speaks during a news conference at the White House in March, 2020. (Reuters: Al Drago)

" And at that show trial, we heard some of the most ghastly, horrific anti-vaccine disinformation I've ever heard. "

Republican committee members accused Dr Fauci of hiding evidence about the dangers of COVID vaccines, destroying public trust in health institutions, and even of helping to create COVID via US funding of a Chinese lab in Wuhan.

"Oh, just a ridiculous conspiracy theory, with no evidence, data, or proof, that Republicans are just hanging onto," Dr Yamey said.

"We know that the most likely cause of this pandemic is a zoonosis, that it came from an animal source."

Sharon Lewin, one of Australia's top infectious diseases experts, said the treatment of Dr Fauci "does a lot of damage".

Anthony Fauci with Sharon Lewin. (Supplied: Doherty Institute)

"The erosion of trust is something that's very, very significant," she said.

"If we had a big pandemic now we'd be asking the public to do all sorts of things, to work in partnership to respond to it, and we need that trust."

Dr Benjamin warned it could lead people to "not follow the advice that they're getting".

"We're already having a lot more vaccine misinformation happen in the United States," he said.

"And if you actually look at the places that followed good evidence, their morbidity and mortality was much less than in those places where they demonised or politicised the response."

Kindergarten vaccination rates in the US are dropping, and earlier this month the US president signed an executive order calling for American children to be vaccinated against fewer diseases.

'Didn't do anything wrong'

Anthony Fauci was director of the US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases from 1984 to 2022. (AP: Al Drago)

Dr Fauci led the scientific response to COVID-19 in the US and was the key presidential advisor on the pandemic.

He advocated mask-wearing and social distancing and urged Americans to get vaccinated as quickly as possible.

"All of this is going to affect people's trusts in vaccines," Dr Yamey said.

"We know that hundreds of thousands of people died. They'd be alive today if they took a vaccine."

The US Center for Disease Control reports that more than 1.2 million Americans died of COVID-19.

Australia's Professor Lewin led research on the diagnosis and treatment of COVID-19 and liaised closely with Dr Fauci during the early stages of the pandemic.

Sharon Lewin says she's "really alarmed" by what is happening to Anthony Fauci. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

"I am really alarmed, largely because of what great contribution Dr Fauci has made over multiple decades in public health, serving under seven presidents with distinction, a person with the highest integrity, commitment to science and truth," she said.

Dr Yamey said Dr Fauci was "a man with over 50 years of really extraordinary public service who got America through previous outbreaks and pandemics, SARS, the anthrax attacks, flu pandemics".

Dr Fauci became director of America's National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases in 1984, when another global pandemic was at its height.

"He had a huge role to play in turning HIV from what was an almost-always fatal disease into something that people can live a normal life with," Dr Yamey said.

Donald Trump speaks about COVID-19 in February 2020 with Anthony Fauci by his side. (AP: Carolyn Kaster)

Dr Benjamin said Dr Fauci "didn't do anything wrong" during COVID.

He said people resented the impositions on their lives during the pandemic.

"You quite frequently had an unnamed, unknown bureaucrat, usually a health official, telling you you needed to stay home, wear a mask and take a shot. And for a while people were okay with that," Dr Benjamin said.

"But then when it began to get in the way of what they wanted to do, people turned on it. And we just weren't very good at risk communication. We could have improved that a lot."

Prison a possibility

Anthony Fauci was the key presidential advisor on the pandemic. (AP Photo: Jacquelyn Martin)

Dr Benjamin said the proper way to examine the response to COVID would be via a national commission similar to the 9/11 Commission, not via politicised public examinations of Dr Fauci.

"I'm actually an emergency physician and I understand disasters and emergencies," Dr Benjamin said.

"And this was a new, emerging disease. We made a lot of assumptions early on that turned out not to be true. And as we learned more, we adjusted just like you would in any disaster … but if we didn't do the things that we did, many, many more people would've died."

The Senate committee investigating Dr Fauci voted to hold him in contempt for refusing to answer questions, and Kentucky senator Rand Paul has referred that resolution to the Justice Department.

Ms Vaughn says that resolution would normally be assessed without political considerations.

But this is a different environment, she said.

Anthony Fauci speaks in front of the Senate committee last month. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

"What I would normally expect is that career prosecutors would evaluate the potential charge, the strengths and the weaknesses, and make a recommendation on what should be done. And the political appointees in the department would be pretty deferential to that," the former prosecutor said.

"From what I see on the outside, it's not clear that that's what would happen here."

In 2022, Ms Vaughn prosecuted former Trump advisor Steve Bannon.

Mr Bannon had refused to testify before Congress over the January 6, 2021 riots.

He refused to attend the hearings, was convicted of contempt and sentenced to four months in jail. The Supreme Court later vacated the charges and sent the case back to the lower courts.

Steve Bannon served four months in prison after being found guilty of contempt of Congress. (Reuters: Kent J Edwards)

Ms Vaughn, who is now in private practice, said Dr Fauci could face a similar sentence if convicted.

"Contempt of Congress is a misdemeanour, and typically I think the maximum is only a year for this offence," she said.

"But in the US we have what are called sentencing guidelines, and that tells a judge what the recommended sentence is. And for crimes like this, for someone like Dr Fauci, it would really be zero to six months.

"That was the range that Mr Bannon was in, and the judge gave him four months there. So I can't imagine that Dr Fauci, if he were to be convicted, would face anything more than that."

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Alleged NDIS fraud plot accused had one-way ticket to Nigeria, court hears
World.content:
A dual citizen charged over his alleged involvement in a $5 million National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) fraud plot had "cut ties" in Adelaide and was preparing to fly to Nigeria before he was arrested, a court has heard.

Foluso Omole appeared in the Adelaide Magistrates Court today where he was refused bail, after Australian Federal Police officers arrested him at Adelaide Airport on Friday.

The court heard Mr Omole, 38, a dual Australian and Nigerian citizen, had "purchased a one-way ticket to Nigeria" before he was arrested as he allegedly prepared to leave the country.

A prosecutor told the court it appeared he had "sent, over the course of his offending, significant funds back to Nigeria" where his wife resides.

The court heard Mr Omole was working as a NDIS coordinator and operated two businesses which employed a number of staff at the time of the alleged offending.

The prosecutor said it was alleged Mr Omole had received "information improperly" from a woman who was employed by the National Disability Insurance Agency over the course of six years, and "used that information to obtain benefit fraudulently".

The court heard she has also been charged with offending and was due to appear in court on Thursday.

The matter was heard in the Adelaide Magistrates Court. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Mr Omole's defence lawyer, Mark Twiggs, told the court his client had informed him that he had been planning to travel on a "return ticket to London" which was "purchased prior to any raid" on the woman's home.

"The charges are denied. He has no record at all," Mr Twiggs said.

"My client has good reason why he should be given bail."

Mr Omole is yet to enter pleas to one count of person deal with proceeds of indictable crime over $1 million and one count of dealing with money/property valued greater than $1 million that is proceeds of crime.

Magistrate Patrick Hill refused bail on the basis that Mr Omole posed a flight risk.

"Whether it was a one-way ticket to Nigeria or a return ticket to London do make a difference as to the court's assessment of whether or not Mr Omole is a flight risk," Mr Hill said.

"For the other reasons put forward by the prosecution, in any event, I remain concerned that he is a risk of flight and the application for bail is refused."

Mr Omole will return to court next month.

World.title: Court hears boy who died sleeping rough in skip bin was missing for days
World.content:
A coronial inquest into the death of a 13-year-old First Nations boy who died after sleeping rough in an industrial skip bin has heard he was missing for five days before his death.

WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the name and image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of their family.

The teenager — whose family has requested that he be referred to as Budda Spencer for cultural reasons — died in May 2021 after a garbage truck driver tipped the bin during a usual collection round in Port Lincoln.

The boy was sleeping alongside two other young boys, aged 11 and 12, who were under the Department for Child Protection's care.

They were not harmed in the incident.

Budda Spencer, 13, died in an incident involving an industrial bin at Port Lincoln in 2021. (Supplied)

Today, special counsel assisting the coroner, Rebecca Schell, told the inquest the boys had made a decision, before Budda Spencer's death, to not return to their respective homes that night.

"The trio had not slept in the bin before this night," Ms Schell said.

"The three boys lay down in the bin in a row. They had planned to stay awake at night but they all fell asleep.

"It was a cold night, but it was warm in the bin and they used cardboard to keep themselves warm."

Flowers and teddy bears were among tributes left near the scene following the horrific incident. (ABC News)

The special counsel said all three boys awoke almost immediately before they were being tipped into the back of the truck.

The court heard one of the younger boys managed to scramble out of the bin to warn the driver.

"[Budda] Spencer attempted to climb out in the same way — [his friend] told him to stay down," Ms Schell said.

The coronial inquest is being held in Port Lincoln. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

The inquest heard Budda Spencer died in the process of trying to escape the garbage truck.

Ms Schell told the court that upon noticing Budda's friend "frantically waving his arms", the driver stopped immediately.

The inquest, which is expected to focus on whether the boy's family had appropriate agency support, is being heard before deputy state coroner Naomi Kereru in Port Lincoln, and will move to Adelaide next week.

Ms Schell told the court the teenager was a "kind, fantastic storyteller who made his friends laugh".

'Was he appropriately supported?'

The court heard that, in the five days before his death when Budda Spencer was missing from home, the boy was spotted at a youth event, and that he had also slept rough at a football oval grandstand in Port Lincoln.

The court heard the police located Budda Spencer during the five-day period and attempted to take him to his house.

"No-one answered the door … and [Budda] Spencer ran off from the police," Ms Schell said.

The circumstances of the incident caused widespread shock. (ABC News)

The court also heard the boy had a good rapport with an OTR petrol station worker who regularly bought him food.

Ms Schell told the court he confided in her, saying "home life was not good".

She said that the night before the boy's death, his two friends were "listed as missing with the police".

Ms Schell said the inquest would consider whether Budda Spencer's family had appropriate support from various organisations in the lead-up to his death.

Budda Spencer's mother Deborah Betts and maternal grandmother leaving the inquest. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

The court heard Budda Spencer's mother Deborah Betts made multiple reports to various agencies about her concerns relating to her son and that she was having trouble making him stay at home.

The inquest is expected to hear from SA Police, West Coast Youth and Community Services, Youth Justice and the Department for Child Protection.

"Was he appropriately supported by various agencies?" Ms Schell said.

"If not, what intervention should have been initiated by the Department for Child Protection?"

Members of Budda Spencer's family outside the coronial inquest, with lawyer Rachael Shaw (right). (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

Ms Betts attended court today with her son's grandmother.

Budda Spencer's aunty also attended, and at times comforted Ms Betts while she heard details about her son's death.

World.title: One Nation flip-flops on migration policy, announces tobacco excise cut
World.content:
PoliticsFederalImmigration One Nation flip-flops on migration policy, announces tobacco excise cut Natassia Chrysanthos and Paul Sakkal Updated August 18, 2026 — 12:06am ,first published 4:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One Nation has been forced to clarify that its migration policy would allow tens of thousands more migrants than it first suggested, raising questions about the rigour of its policy manifesto, as Pauline Hanson pledges to slash the tobacco excise. For months, policy experts and political opponents have scratched their heads about One Nation’s vision for lowering migrant numbers, a hot-button issue that has helped drive Hanson’s popularity. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce at Parliament House. Alex Ellinghausen The minor party will on Tuesday push a plan to lower the tobacco excise by 75 per cent, even as it faces pressure over its core immigration focus. Its policy, as explained on its website, said the party would cut migration “by capping visas at 130,000 per year” to ease pressure on housing and infrastructure. But it had not specified which types of visas. The migration system includes temporary visas, such as students’, working holidaymakers’ and short-term skilled visas, some of which are demand-driven. The government also gives 185,000 permanent visas a year to skilled workers, family reunions and humanitarian cases. A combination of both visa types contributes to the net overseas migration figure – migrants who stay, minus those who depart.



Either way, a policy of 130,000 visas would lead to either zero or negative overall migration since tens of thousands of people leave the country each year. One Nation’s explicit policy before the last election was “net zero” migration, although that term has since been dropped from its website. Related Article Immigration Does One Nation’s migration policy actually add up? But One Nation’s Barnaby Joyce on Monday said the 130,000 figure applied to the net intake of migrants. This would mean the number of visas issued would be much higher than 130,000. Asked by reporters whether One Nation was referring to total visas issued or the net overall migrant intake each year, Joyce said at a press conference on Monday: “It’s net.” It came after Hanson muddied the waters on the weekend when she was grilled on the difference between net migration and the number of permanent visas during a Sunday morning interview on News24’s Sunday Agenda.



At one point Hanson said she wanted “net migration [of] about 130,000”. But in answer to a later question on permanent visas, she said, “I want to see 130,000 as the permanent number that are here.” One Nation had not previously said that its 130,000 figure related to net migration. Party representatives have not responded to this masthead’s questions about the policy in the past, although a spokesperson also told SBS on the weekend that it was a net figure. Loading Hanson also said the country needed better leadership to “turn the country around” and stop people leaving Australia. However, more people staying in Australia for longer would actually increase net overseas migration because it would lead to fewer outflows. One Nation is the political party most trusted to manage immigration, according to a survey of Australians in this masthead’s Resolve Political Monitor.



The party’s policy platform is yet to grapple with the ramifications that deep cuts to migration would have on key workforces, including in regional areas that are emerging as potential electoral strongholds. Separately, One Nation is pledging to cut the tobacco excise by 75 per cent to make legal cigarettes nearly as cheap as those sold on the black market. Hanson will release a new policy on Tuesday promising to cut the excise drastically and pause its indexation for a further three years. Labor has resisted calls from NSW Premier Chris Minns and many experts to cut the excise. Hanson also gazumps the Coalition, which has been formulating a policy on tobacco tax for months, although her policy was not costed. Promising to “break the black market”, Hanson presented party analysis stating a $46 legal pack would fall to about $21. Illicit packs are normally sold at between $12 to $25, the policy states. “Our plan makes legal tobacco competitive and attacks the gangs’ extraordinary profit margin,” Hanson said in a statement.



“People are sick of the firebombing, shootings, extortion and killings. They are sick of watching tobacco shops burn, while organised crime takes control of the market. On migration, Farrer MP David Farley, during this year’s byelection, broke with party policy during a candidate forum by suggesting it was “probably not” an issue if Australia’s net migration reached 306,000. “If we’re successful in One Nation’s water policies, we’re going to need more labour, and we’re going to need more labour quickly, skilled labour,” he said. Related Article Exclusive

Resolve Political Monitor Labor marked down on migration as delayed visa shake-up approaches Last week, Liberal frontbencher Andrew Bragg sparked confusion about the Coalition’s net overseas migration target by suggesting it would be about 180,000. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor initially offered a figure below 200,000 but said he did not want to commit until he knew how many houses were built before the next election. Days later, Taylor told The Australian its figure would be about 173,000, based on the current rate at which homes were being built. The Australian also reported that One Nation wanted to ban entrants from countries that were on the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade’s “do not travel” list, such as Lebanon, Palestine, Afghanistan and Russia.



Joyce on Monday, however, suggested it was not an all-out ban. “People are saying we’re just completely ruling out certain areas. That’s not the case. We’re talking about greater stringencies,” he said. In a rare intervention into domestic politics, the consulate for Haiti in Australia contested One Nation’s policy on behalf of the tiny diaspora. In an open letter to Hanson, honorary consul Julia Melamed said she had difficulty with “the idea that a travel advisory written about a country can serve as a judgment on the people who come from it”. “We know of no conduct within this community that would justify calling Haitians in Australia a security concern,” she wrote. “People who leave a country in crisis are not usually carrying that crisis with them; they are trying to get away from it … We ask you, senator, and everyone taking part in this debate, to keep two ideas separate.” Labor has also been agonising over a policy to cut net overseas migration from 300,000 to 225,000, though it has struggled to land the final package over concerns about offending migrant communities and creating economic harm. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: No truck with terrorism
World.content:
The latest missive from Chris Henning of Rozelle, his first since the COVID days, is headed “A Very Important Question”, and so it is: “If whichever Boeing 747 President Trump travels in becomes automatically Air Force One by virtue of his presence, does that mean that the catering van in which he was recently moved secretly to a secure alternative plane was, while he was inside, Food Truck One? I think the public deserves to know.” Excellent to hear from you, Chris. It’s good to stay in touch.

“My husband, who likes sailing, and I couldn’t help but bag out All Is Lost, a sea survival movie starring Robert Redford that must be the worst ‘silent’ movie (C8) we’ve seen,” attests Merilyn McClung of Forestville. “Unbelievable from start to finish with nothing said except for the final scene, where he utters the f-word. Anyone who sails would know there would be much more salty language.”

“In the early ’70s, my husband was denied entry (C8) to a restaurant for not wearing a tie,” writes Helen Howes of Collaroy. “Although at that time restaurants and clubs frequently kept a collection of ties, and sometimes jackets, on hand to fulfil the dress code, his shirt was in a (thankfully) short-lived fashion for a high polo-neck, made of normal cotton shirt material, with buttons at the nape, so nowhere to properly put a tie without it looking like a hangman’s noose. We ate elsewhere.”

Lyn Langtry of East Ryde says that “in 1975 in Glastonbury, Somerset, my friend with a fashionable Afro hairstyle had difficulty in finding accommodation because she was considered a hippie and hippies weren’t considered desirable guests in some establishments”. Granny can’t help wondering what they did when Marc Bolan turned up there in 1970.

“I can attest that it is true, crossing by overnight boat from Sumatra to Penang in 1975 there was a communal trimming of hair and smartening of clothing in fear of the dreaded S.H.I.T. stamp and the 48 hours to get out of Malaysia,” recalls Graham Cochrane of Balmain.

World.title: The LNP wants more police, not MPs. Expert says it’s a ‘false economy’
World.content:
Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: a case for democratic improvement, State Development shareholdings, looming teacher pay talks, and the simmering four-day week. People don’t like the idea of more politicians, according to the widely held belief. Some people also dislike vegetables, but the consequences of going without are not ideal. And if your doctor suggested you should eat more vegetables, you’d listen – right? The Clerk of Queensland Parliament, Neil Laurie, during an estimates hearing last month. Queensland Parliament In this metaphor, the doctor is the Clerk of the Parliament of Queensland, Neil Laurie, who has held the top parliamentary service job since 2003.





While proud of the reform he has been part of, and not reflecting on any particular parliament or government, Laurie wrote he is “neither blind nor mute about the institution’s weaknesses”. Laurie said an upper house would need to be designed properly but, ultimately, would be unlikely to occur due to the need for a referendum and bipartisan support. Instead, he floats constitutional entrenchment of safeguards, including super-majority style votes to rush bills or add unrelated last-minute amendments. But he also suggests lifting the number of MPs in parliament to make up for decades of unmatched population growth putting pressure on its ability to properly fulfil its functions.



The usual argument against this on costs is a “false economy”, Laurie says, because an extra $35 million a year – at least – is now being spent supporting strained MPs and their offices. That’s compared with an estimated cost of $1 million a year for a new MP, office and staff. For Laurie, another non-upper house reform would be bolstering the government-controlled committee system, which has changed little in 15 years. The last review of that, a decade ago this year, held its punches to allow the changes to “slowly evolve and develop”. Develop they have, but not all in a positive direction.





More answers – and curiosities – in State Development chief shares The changing of the guards at State Development is complete, as newly minted director-general David Mackie officially gets his knees under the desk for the five-year term. Both former State Development director-general John Sosso and his successor, former public sector commissioner David Mackie, until recently held shares in a uranium mining company with the largest deposits in the state – despite a ban on their extraction. Sosso left still doing so. (Circus is yet to receive a hint of a response from Premier David Crisafulli’s team about the appointment process after numerous nudges.) The news presents an opportunity to share an update to an earlier question we’d asked the government: specifically, the Queensland uranium shareholdings of Mackie’s predecessor John Sosso.



While Mackie has spent this year offloading potentially tricky shares ahead of a sideways move to serve under his marriage celebrant and minister, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie, Sosso held on. Sosso, through the department, had previously refused to answer our questions about when he purchased the shares. Through the magic of Right to Information, we can narrow the window. Department bosses have had to declare their interests for decades, though it wasn’t until the Palaszczuk government that such disclosures became public-facing. Through this scheme, we were able to nail down Mackie’s purchase of shares in Paladin Energy to July 2021, while he was leading the Justice Department. (We suggest no wrongdoing by him or Sosso.) Paladin, one of three firms in which Mackie and Sosso held shares, lays claim to the largest uranium reserves in Queensland – although mining the resource remains banned in the state.



Readers will know that before Sosso’s return to the state public sector at the 2024 change of government, he headed up Justice under then attorney-general Bleijie in the Newman era. Related Article Exclusive

Public service ‘Creates a smell’: Top bureaucrat urged to detail shares in uranium miner The goods from Circus’ RTI request for Sosso’s declarations of interests from this time show he held no shares coming into the role, and filed an update adding Commonwealth Bank shares in mid-2014. Speaking of shares, the declaration from (former) acting State Development chief Shaun Ferris had him take the title during his short-lived term atop the department as the only DG with shares in Tesla, Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey’s Block Inc, and bitcoin. The more you know.



Teachers’ day in court looms for first pay rise in more than a year We’re now well over a year since the expiry of a workplace deal between state school teachers and the government – which means a year without the pay rise that would come from a renewed one. And the next date in the ensuing industrial court dance between the teachers’ union and the Education Department looms (before your next Circus edition) on Monday, August 24. In it, the parties will hash it out not over the broader deal, but a 3 per cent interim pay case. Negotiations between the state and the Queensland Teachers’ Union (QTU) fell apart in June last year, leading to a statewide strike last August.



In October, the state made what Education Minister John-Paul Langbroek called its “best and final offer” to the union. The offer was summarily rejected by voting members, and by early November, the QTU threatened (and then carried out) a second strike, alongside rolling work bans and industrial action. Queensland teachers gather in Queen’s Park during the second of two Queensland Teachers’ Union strike days last year. Polina Levina/Getty Images A letter from Education Department director-general Sharon Schimming leaked to media outlined several asks from the union to halt the further strike action in late 2025. Those requests included ditching matters the union considered well-trodden ground, and including the interim wage increase in line with wages policy – which the department rejected.



Langbroek warned at the time it could take months for arbitration of the case to make it to the industrial court, with repeated warnings from the state the process could take up to two years. While teachers across several pay brackets hit the award threshold in late 2025 – triggering minor pay bumps – the state has remained steadfast against any pay increase outside a new EBA. Langbroek reiterated this point during his recent estimates appearance, saying that while the state wasn’t opposed to wage increases in line with wages policy, it was opposed to this one. This was because of, in the minister’s words, “the wide scope of the claim and the likely effect on the employer and employees” with an interim pay rise an “arbitrary figure” while parties waited for an Industrial Relations Commission ruling. Miles pumps brakes on talk of four-day public sector work week



It’s the simmering push that keeps bubbling up: a four-day week in the Queensland public sector. Related Article Public service The official David Crisafulli calls direct (just don’t say he bypasses Dale Last) Fresh from a fuel-price linked approach by the Australian Services Union in March, outlined in Circus and promptly waved away by the Crisafulli government, the idea is back. This time, the idea of a shorter week for the same pay has emerged as an element of the draft policy platform getting around before the state Labor conference at the end of the month. As laid bare by our column comrades Chooks, the draft form of the now ACTU-backed effort would ask a state Labor government to trial a four-day week in sections of the public sector before a progressive expansion push through legislation and lobbying with industries and unions.



While a spinner for Opposition Leader Steven Miles had said the pitch showed his party was the only one concerned about working Queenslanders, the man himself qualified things a tad more. “Let’s not get too far ahead of ourselves,” Miles said, noting it was a draft to be hashed out over two of the annual Labor gatherings before a call was made on what would be taken to the 2028 election. “[It’s] not something that we’d be open to implementing in any kind of statewide fashion.” Have a curiosity for the Circus tent? Email us on m.dennien@nine.com.au or james.hall@nine.com.au. For more security, sing out with a non-work device and network via Signal (mattdennien.15 or here) and mattdennien@protonmail.com.
