World.title: How will Jess Wilson cut debt without cutting services?
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters How will Jess Wilson cut debt without cutting services? August 17, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Cathy Wilcox To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. STATE ELECTION The Victorian Coalition has now committed to spending $90 million a year to save some of us (predominantly in marginal seats) toll charges (“Road tolls to be capped at $50 weekly under Coalition commuter plan”, 16/7). Rural voters must be ecstatic about paying more taxes to subsidise Melbourne.

It would help if they could now explain how they’ll keep their commitment to reduce the state debt (by an albeit minuscule 1 per cent per annum) by doing that, when they are also spending $250 million extra per year on potholes, cancelling the ESL, lowering payroll tax, getting rid of land tax and employing thousands more police and PSOs (if they can get them) – without cutting services or sacking public servants.

Maybe it explains why their social media posts now talk about “stabilising” debt rather than reducing it, as they have until recently.

Richard Jamonts, Williamstown Pledge gives help to those who don’t need it

Jess Wilson’s cap on toll fees considers, like so much policy, that the cost-of-living crisis is experienced by everyone equally.

Why give a motorist on $800,000 a year the same help as someone on $80,000? Such general applications assist those who don’t need it while reducing the pool of what might be made to those in real need of financial assistance.

Jenny Herbert, Metung



Wilson gives low priority to sustainability

Victorian Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has made a number of announcements which focus on the the cost of living but indicate the low priority her Coalition give to sustainability.

Bringing back weekly bin collections ignores the benefits of lowering the amount of waste going into landfill and increases costs to councils. The opposition say they will “end the gas ban” but helping switch Victorian households to more efficient electric technology will have economy wide benefits, reduce harmful pollution and increase energy security.

They say they will run coal plants for as long as possible, locking in more pollution and climate harm for our communities and raising insurance costs.

Nature is under increasing pressure and climate risk is rising. Hip-pocket announcements may be popular, but I don’t think these policies will make Victoria “safer or more affordable” in the long run.

David Hudspeth, Burwood Grid costs are a major part of power bills

The good news is that “record-breaking renewable energy generation” has helped many customers, with lower bills. The bad news is that the grid will continue to require major investment (″⁣Energy giants warn big test still to come for power grid″⁣, 17/8).

The Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) confirms that the cheapest way to maintain grid reliability is with wind and solar, backed up by batteries, hydroelectric and some gas.

LNP energy policy includes building more rooftop solar and battery installations in urban areas. There would be major impacts of Jess Wilson’s promise to protect farmers by “pausing major transmission projects”. Whatever the chosen energy mix, grid costs are a major part of power bills.

John Hughes, Mentone Why does all the money go to one firm?

In the same edition, The Age reports that a private-sector consortium is circling to get the inside running on building the airport rail link (″⁣Private sector weighs bid to help Melbourne’s airport rail link finally take off″⁣, 16/8). We also read that the Coalition will use our taxes to subsidise Transurban tolls. One may have hoped the Coalition would offer a government that would rein in such cosy deals. If cost-of-living pressures are such that commuters require assistance, why should all the money be directed to one firm? .

Eric Keys, retired transport planner, Flemington Tawdry vote grab

What a ridiculous idea of the state Coalition to reimburse tolls of up to $3000 per year. It makes one wonder if the Coalition would be any better at government than the current lot. This is nothing more than a tawdry attempt at vote grabbing, something that we are more than used to in Australia. It means all Victorians will pay, instead of the toll road users.

This considered action has nothing to do with Transurban, and it does not deserve criticism as it only operates the roads and will receive normal payments due. Keep in mind, Melbourne would not have the freeway network we currently have if it was not for the toll operator.

Mike Weiss, Vermont South THE FORUM



Small business lament

The proposed changes to the tax system, especially the changes to trusts will decimate small business. However, this is hardly mentioned in the media or by politicians. Small business accounts for half of all business output in Australia.

Farmers have a strong voice in the National Farmers’ Federation and the Nationals, and have successfully argued for a carve-out from the tax changes. But why do these 400,000 small businesses that operate through trusts not receive the same consideration? Because they don’t have a voice. (When was the last time anyone saw a headline from the Council of Small Business Organisations Australia or even know who COSBOA is?)

And so, democracy fails. The single vote of a coffee shop owner is valued the same as a public servant who wants to retain “work from home” privileges, or a uni student who votes for HECS fee relief, or the salary worker who demands childcare rebates.

None of these voters care about the changes to the tax system. And so the crucial engine of economic growth in our community will pack up and leave. And we will, as a nation, be all the poorer for it.

Wayne Alexander, Eltham COVID not the problem

Neil Mitchell’s article (″⁣There’s a nasty mood festering in this state″⁣, 16/8) describes the negative society in which we live. Various reasons for the anger and resentment are postulated, such as a hangover from the pandemic. The pandemic privations – there were many– finished almost five years ago.

Blaming the pandemic cannot continue: we can and should be over this. Those who lived through WWII, especially those survivors of Japanese POW horrors who came home and got on with it, worked to rebuild their lives without the anger and appalling behaviour demonstrated now.

The negativity of the press – eg. describing Victoria as a ″⁣rust bucket″⁣ – contributes to disaffection, as does the focus on trivia: ″⁣melongate″⁣. General ignorance is a problem – in an age where the wisdom of the world is available with a click of a few buttons, far too many people look to lies and false ″⁣information″⁣, forming opinions which are simply wrong.

Louise Kloot, Doncaster Rich and poor divide

As we approach our state election in November, columnist Neil Mitchell seems to skip over the fact that this anger is not just in our state, or our country, but a mood expressed throughout the “free” world.

Among a list of possible reasons, he leans heavily on the aftereffects of Victoria’s onerous COVID lockdowns. This doesn’t explain why populists whipping up anger are rising in most Western nations. How about the huge wealth gap that has opened in these countries? The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare cites several studies showing wealth inequality significantly reduces happiness in a society. We watch as the “so-called” leader of the free world uses his position of power to enrich himself and his cronies and cuts aid to desperate people on or below the breadline.

Closer to home, who wouldn’t be angry to see our taxpayer dollars fed to already wealthy private schools while the schools their children attend are unable to cover even the most basic necessities?

There are many struggling families in Australia, and it is hard to imagine that this anger won’t continue while they see their “well-off” neighbours enjoying many advantages not available to themselves, not to mention the billionaires able to consistently multiply their wealth every year.

The Albanese government’s recent changes to tax breaks for the wealthy and those with investment properties are steps in the right direction to address the wealth gap. Much more needs to be done at state and federal levels, however. Let us start looking for solutions, rather than blame.

Jan Downing, Hawthorn East Elephant in room

I would suggest that Neil Mitchell’s article (16/8) misses the elephant in the room. Is Victoria much different to the US or UK? What do these places have in common? The failed and selfish economic agenda called neo-liberalism. Oh, and then the columnist’s irony to quote the Centre for Independent Studies, a bastion of free-market individualism.

Phil Labrum, Trentham



Saw it coming

On reading “The Emerald Isle has turned yellow as food supply fears rise across Europe” (16/8), I’m reminded of an ABC Radio National report 20 years ago in which Philip Adams interviewed a British climate scientist who said the British Isles and Europe would face a semi-arid climate within a century.

He said people can live in semi-arid climates but that the population supported would be substantially less that at present and that if carbon emissions were stopped immediately, it would take at least a century for the atmosphere to repair. I think that this summer in Europe is illustrating that the prophesies made are coming to pass.

Christopher Jarvis, Point Lonsdale Living in hotboxes

Many years ago, during an intense heatwave, my late mother-in-law came perilously close to death. She was in her post-war weatherboard house with poor insulation, and, by the third day of heat, with her air conditioner malfunctioning, her house was an inferno.

Hearing her weak voice on the phone we rushed to her side with a fan, wet towels and ice cubes and were able to cool her before the excellent ambulance members came. They were surprised she was alive.

There are thousands of homes of the type she lived in still being used in Melbourne today. They are hotboxes in summer and freezing in the winter. There are also a remarkable number of later built houses and units with no trees or eaves for shading.

To hear Coalition shadow ministers suggest we build lower quality houses is madness. Heat waves are raging in Europe and people are dying in their apartments that were designed for a totally different climate.

Houses built now will still be there in 40 years when the climate will be hotter still.

Helen Hook, Black Rock Yielding to idiom

“The reason why” used in journalist Nikki Barrowclough’s first sentence (″⁣There’s no getting around it: We need to talk about this irksome word″⁣, 15/8) is a tautology but nonetheless has become somewhat idiomatic. At what point does prescriptive grammar yield to idiom?

There are many phrases in English whose origins are obscure and which are not capable of grammatical deconstruction. The writer’s use of ″⁣reticent″⁣ rather than ″⁣reluctant″⁣ is indicative of the way in which words whose meaning once clearly delineated are now becoming interchangeable. The word none can mean no-one or not any as one wishes.

Justin Mackenzie, Sassafras Immigration question

Has federal Labor left its run too late on immigration? (“Labor marked down on migration as delayed visa shake-up approaches”, 17/8). In the last stages of Joe Biden’s presidency, it finally dawned that his open door immigration policy was failing, and he rushed in measures to change it, but too late. In the US public’s mind, Biden was soft on immigration and he and the Democrats suffered as a result.

Perceptions in politics take a while to develop, but once they do, they are hard to eradicate. Labor needs a bold, plain statement signalling to the electorate that it is taking charge of this mismanaged system with a new policy framework: sustainable, transparent and catering to the interests of all Australians – not just the business class, whose interests in a high immigration intake are clearly self-serving.

Greg Gardiner, Brunswick Punching the ball

Sports journalist Michael Gleeson’s explanation that you can’t punch your own ball through for a score after the siren has not always been upheld by the league (″⁣The AFL’s quirky rule exposed amid frenzy of Saturday night’s draw″⁣, 17/8).

At round 1, 1982, Carlton v Fitzroy at Princes Park, Mario Bortolotto punched the ball through for a score to Carlton and the match resulted in a draw.

The technical ruling was that the trajectory of the ball would have taken it through even if Mario hadn’t punched it, and as such the goal umpire adjudicated the punch had not assisted the score. Goal umpires back then must have had a type of ESP.

Stephen Turner, Quarry Hill



Denton a class act

Thank you to the Logies awards for recognising the extraordinary talent of Andrew Denton whose strength was guiding guests to step away from their protective public personas and being authentic. It made for extraordinary viewing on Denton Unplugged.

It was a masterclass of extensive research to see what others say about them, including many celebrities who hide behind their PR machines and don’t usually go off script. His shows never insulted the intelligence of his TV audience, and for that I am extremely grateful, providing us with so many memorable moments.

Sally Walcock, Toorak AND ANOTHER THING Matt Golding Accolades

My faith is restored. Muster Dogs won a Logie.

Heather Barker, Albert Park



Andrew Denton’s acceptance speech for his Logie Hall of Fame award was full of grace, humour and humility. Politicians of every ilk should be forced to watch it!

Peter Venn, East Bentleigh Will Pauline Hanson now request an official enquiry into Shane Jacobson’s joke about her at The Logies? If Gina Rinehart gets offended at jokes at her expense, will Pauline follow in the same manner, or do commercial networks get a free pass ?

Jenny Smith, East Melbourne Can I kindly remind Dave Hughes of the infamous speech by Ricky Gervais at the Golden Globes where he called out the hypocrisy of privileged celebrities: ″⁣You’re in no position to lecture the public about anything as you don’t live in the real world ... you’ve spent less time in school than Greta Thunberg″⁣.

Pamela Papadopoulos, South Yarra Cricket

Good to see only whole numbers used on the report card for Australia’s Test cricketers. Food critics and others, please take note (“Australia player ratings after shock Test loss to Bangladesh”, 17/8).

The use of half marks is pretentious and unnecessary when the mark is already out of 5, 10 or 20.

Lindsay Zoch, Mildura Surely, it’s no coincidence that Australia’s capitulation to Bangladesh occurred in Darwin, whereby Bangladesh best adapted to an old-fashioned notion of preparing for a five-day Test match.

The folly of the Aussies was to rely upon hubris, the downfall of many who have come before.

Tim Goddard, Barwon Heads



Finally

Musk has left his prediction re a future without money too late (″⁣Why the richest man on Earth wants you to think money won’t matter″⁣, 16/8).

l have been living without money three days a week for years.

James Lane, Hampton East The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Revealed: The Swans players who could be stood down on finals eve amid sexual assault investigation
World.content:
Key Sydney Swans players are at the centre of a Victoria Police sexual assault investigation putting their immediate playing futures under a cloud and plunging the club’s finals campaign into turmoil. The investigation relates to an allegation of sexual assault at an East Melbourne hotel hours after the team’s victory over Essendon at the MCG on Sunday night. Loading This masthead has contacted the representatives of Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice, James Jordon, Chad Warner and one other player after two senior industry sources said they were spoken to by police after an allegation of sexual assault in the early hours of Monday morning. This masthead is not suggesting all five players are under investigation by police, just that they are assisting with enquiries. The group of five were driving home to Sydney in a rental car on Monday night.



A manager representing a fifth player denied his client was one of the players involved. The five players are unlikely to play this week regardless of the police investigation, as the Swans consider potential sanctions for late-night drinking at the team hotel, which is funded by the AFL, after a match. Chad Warner (left), Isaac Heeney (right), James Jordon (middle bottom) and Riley Bice (middle top) of the Swans. Michael Howard Asked whether they were considering standing down the players, the Swans said all options were open as they worked through the facts of what happened. This was confirmed by a senior AFL source. The players were not arrested. Police asked to review CCTV footage from the Pullman East Melbourne as part of their investigation.



Plain clothes officers went inside hotel rooms and left the venue with a number of items in evidence bags, according to a witness to the police visit. They also asked for footage from cameras that cover public areas of the hotel such as the lobby, stairs and lifts. The Swans have been left “shocked and disappointed” amid the investigation, which focuses on the actions of a group of players in the early hours of Monday morning. Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich fronts the media on Monday. Sitthixay Ditthavong The team was staying at the Pullman after their victory over Essendon at the nearby MCG. Sydney chief executive Matthew Pavlich briefly fronted media in Sydney on Monday to address the alleged incident.



“We’re still piecing together exactly what’s transpired here and have our own set of internal inquiries ongoing. It’s safe to say that we’re extremely shocked and disappointed that this has taken place and that the players have found themselves in this situation,” Pavlich said. “We understand the level of interest in the matter. There’s going to be lots of speculation, but given it’s a police matter right now, that is all that we can say.” The Pullman hotel in East Melbourne. Simon Schluter Pavlich did not take questions, and did not respond to a reporter’s question about whether or not arrests had been made. Two industry sources, speaking anonymously because the investigation is ongoing, said the players were driving back to Sydney on Monday evening to avoid media at Melbourne and Sydney airports.



The AFL held discussions with the Swans on Monday about whether the club would identify the players, and about whether they would be available to play in the coming weeks. One photo being shared in chat groups, showing a woman with damaged teeth, does not relate to the incident. It was published by tabloid news sites in the UK earlier this year, months before the incident. Police with clipboards and camera equipment were seen in the lobby of the hotel on Monday morning. Pullman hotel staff would not comment.



Victoria Police confirmed they were “investigating a report of a sexual assault in East Melbourne on August 17”. “The incident occurred at a hotel on Wellington Parade in the early hours of the morning,” it said in a statement. “The exact circumstances are yet to be established and the investigation into the incident remains ongoing.” Swans board member and club great Michael O’Loughlin was spotted at Sydney’s domestic airport on Monday but declined to shed further light on the matter when approached for comment. “No, we’ll wait and see what the findings are, I don’t know,” O’Loughlin said.



Related Article Investigation

AFL off-field behaviour Hidden boardrooms, crime threats and nude pics: Inside the AFL’s most secretive unit Earlier on Monday the Swans released a statement. “The Sydney Swans can confirm several players were involved in an alleged incident in Melbourne last night,” the club confirmed in a statement on Monday. “The Swans have notified the AFL and relevant authorities and cannot provide further comment at this stage.” The AFL confirmed the league had been notified by the Swans and said the matter rested with police.



In cases such as this, the AFL’s integrity unit defers to police. The Swans are second on the ladder and well-placed to contend for the premiership with 17 wins, with one home-and-away round left before finals. They are due to play North Melbourne next Sunday in Sydney. Unlike the NRL, the AFL does not have a no-fault stand down rule for players charged with serious offences. However, Geelong’s Tanner Bruhn did not play for the Cats in 2025 after he was charged with rape and intentional sexual touching. The charges were dropped last November after a key witness admitted to lying, and Bruhn’s name was suppressed until the case was discontinued. St Kilda sacked Andrew Lovett after he was charged with rape in 2010, terminating his contract over “a series of acts and omissions in breach of his employment contract”. He was later found not guilty of the rape charge.



In 2013, St Kilda player Stephen Milne took an indefinite leave of absence from the club after he was charged with three counts of rape. The charges were dropped when Milne instead pleaded guilty to a single charge of indecent assault. The Sydney players have not been arrested or charged with any offence. With Marc McGowan Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Defence force launches new drone training programme
World.content:
The army has launched a new training course for building drones with 3D printers and flying them - including as if they were armed.

The NZ Defence Force plans to spend up to several hundred million dollars on drones in the next three years.

Its latest three-week course teaches soldiers to deploy and repair drones cheaply in the field.

Qualified drone operators can use the course to increase their skills with the technology. While they will mostly train on surveillance and reconnaissance, commanding officer Lieutenant Colonel Jerry Mateparae said it went beyond that.

"We are not flying UAS with live explosives, but it is clearly a mature technology now that is being used in current conflicts, so we are future-proofing our needs by developing the skills to be able to do this."

The course is based on an Australian model from its Land Combat College and has instructors from over the Tasman to boost inter-operability.

The Australian Army has talked about being "ready to kill enemy personnel with their lethal payloads".

World.title: Our Changing World: A precious piece of sediment and what it says about our future
World.content:
A precious piece of sediment, and what it says about our future Our Changing World Download MP3 30m

Follow Our Changing World on Apple, Spotify, iHeartRadio or wherever you listen to your podcasts

It's mid-June and in a cold, echo-filled warehouse space on the University of Otago campus an international team of scientists and technicians has gathered.

For a moment the deafening sound of a diamond blade saw slicing through sediment and rock drowns everything, before the background chatter of different researchers hunkered over benches, discussing findings, re-emerges.

This is the Otago Repository for Core Analysis, nicknamed ORCA, and for these two weeks it is hosting a rare and hard-won core of sediment retrieved from under the ice in Antarctica.

A cylinder of sediment that the team hopes will help us understand what will happen as our climate warms.

The Otago Repository for Core Analysis (ORCA) is a specially-designed facility to allow this kind of work. RNZ / Claire Concannon

The precious sediment core

There are a number of reasons why the team in ORCA are so excited about this particular tube of rock and mud.

After two failed attempts in the two previous years, this was the third go at retrieving such a core.

The previous failures came down to technical reasons, but there's no doubt the team had set themselves an unprecentented and extremely difficult task.

Drillers pull a core to the surface. Ana Tovey SWAIS2C

The 218 metres of sediment they finally recovered (a record-breaking length) was only drilled after they'd used hot water to melt a hole through 523 metres of ice, all at a distance of about 700km away from the nearest base.

But perhaps the number one reason for the excitement is where the sediment has come from, and the story it can tell about how this part of Antarctica has changed in the past.

Some of the team with the core that passed 200m - a record breaking amount of core from under the ice. Ana Tovey SWAIS2C

Their drill site was at a place called Crary Ice Rise where a finger of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet juts out, still sitting on the bedrock of the Antarctic continent.

This ice sheet is essentially a massive glacier, sitting on the rock. Where it meets ocean the ice flows off the land to float on the seawater, forming an ice shelf, hundreds of metres thick.

When the ice sheet shrinks it ultimately results in more fresh water being added to the ocean, contributing to sea level rise globally.

So the question this massive international project wanted to answer was: what has happened to the ice sheet in the past, at times when our climate was much warmer? And can this help us predict what is coming our way?

'Like you read a book'

Earth Sciences New Zealand's Dr Georgia Grant was on the ice when the core started to come up - a "pinch yourself" moment for her.

A sedimentologist, Georgia says her training allows her to read in the rocks the clues of what's happened in that area across time.

Sedimentologist Dr Georgia Grant describes the colour and grain size of the core. RNZ / Claire Concannon

Different types of sediments found in the core point to different past environments.

In open ocean, fine particles and microfossils settle gently to the seafloor. Larger stones found in that sediment may have been dropped by melting icebergs.

But when an ice sheet is directly involved, it can grind and mix everything together - from fine glacial flour to cobbles and boulders.

"Ice causes chaos," says Georgia. "But again, in a very particular way, in a way that is recognisable."

The core they recovered has the telltale signs of both the presence of ice and open water. Near the bottom, the oldest part of the core, they found microfossil-rich muds from a warmer time period, followed by a long section where ice was present, and then the muds indicating open ocean again higher in the core.

Key then is to figure out the age of the different sections of the core, so that they can be lined up with existing evidence of what was happening to the climate and environment at the time.

Dating the sediment

Amy Leventer from Colgate University has swapped a New York summer for a Dunedin winter to sit in front of a microscope to study microfossils.

Part of the biostratigraphy team, she's doing some of the important work of dating the sediments using the remains of tiny single-celled photosynthetic algae called diatoms. Diatoms make their shells out of silica and are common in such polar marine sediments.

Amy Leventer samples some of the working half of the core to look for microfossils. Ana Tovey SWAIS2C

Decades of research has established time constraints for different species of diatoms, says Amy.

"We use microfossils that have first appearances and last appearances. We know when they lived. And so when we observe them, we can pretty precisely tell... the age of the material."

Age estimates show most of the recovered core spans 7-10 million years ago, with the final 20 metres at the bottom dating back to 17 - 19 million years ago.

This overlaps with a geological time period called the Miocene (23 - 5 million years ago), for which there are some data sets on carbon dioxide levels and estimates of ocean temperatures determined using chemical proxies, as well as models for what the temperatures would have been across that time.

Because it is a massive stretch of time there are significant changes within the Miocene, but in general it was a period much warmer relative to today, by at least three degrees.

What it means for our future

The Paris Climate Agreement aims to hold global warming well below 2 degrees, but the Climate Action Tracker website currently says global policies put us on track for a 2.6 degree rise by 2100.

One of the questions the project set out to answer was around the sensitivity of the West Antarctic Ice Sheet to 2 degrees of warming.

The team slept in tents on the Ross Ice Shelf Ana Tovey SWAIS2C

They wanted to investigate this by looking back to the middle Pliocene, around three million years ago, when average global temperatures were 2-3 degrees warmer.

They didn't collect sediments of that age in this core, but they hope to find the resources to return to another site which they suspect might have those younger sediments.

So while open ocean in this part of Antarctica might not be in our immediate future, co-chief scientist Associate Professor Huw Horgan still found it a challenging sight when the core started coming to the surface.

"It was confronting, where we're over 500 kilometres from the open ocean. We had this huge ice shelf between us that that has been there for all of human history. We've only known that ice shelf to be there. And yet here we are looking at a record from 82 degrees south with no ice shelf."

Initial investigations of the more subtle evidence suggested there was still ice nearby, with further ongoing study they hope to get a clearer picture of the changes in this part of Antarctica across the time period they've collected.

Co-chief scientist Professor Molly Patterson holds a length of packaged core. Ana Tovey SWAIS2C

While it is a significant sediment record, it is still just from one point, right on the edge of the ice sheet, says co-chief scientist Associate Professor Molly Patterson. She says it would help to have more sediment cores from other areas.

While Associate Professor Huw Horgan agrees, when it comes to the question of what should ideally happen next, his answer is simple.

"In an ideal world we would stop warming the planet."

World.title: Datagrid begins work on Southland site, completion expected this year
World.content:
The company behind plans for the country's largest data centre says building work begins Tuesday on the 49ha site in Makarewa, north of Invercargill.

Singapore-based Datagrid said the start of the "horizontal works" marked a major milestone in the project. It said New Zealand company HEB Construction - a subsidiary of international firm, VINCI Construction - had been contracted to carry out the work.

Datagrid said the works included a new access road connecting the data centre campus to State Highway 98 and upgrading existing roads.

Topsoil on the data centre site would be excavated and used to create a six-metre-high bund, which the company said would help shield the local community from construction noise.

It said the foundation platform for the future AI data centre facility, cable landing station and power substation were expected to be completed by the end of the year.

Datagrid NZ chief executive Rémi Galasso said the project's timeline was ambitious.

"Datagrid won't just be the largest data centre project in New Zealand, but also one of the most sustainable data centre projects of that scale in the Asia Pacific. We hope to demonstrate that New Zealand has all the ingredients to be a world champion in this industry."

Opponents of the $3.5 billion project worry about the centre's environmental impact, water use and noise pollution.

Last month, hundreds of people packed a meeting, organised by the Southland Sustainable Resource Coalition, to voice their concerns.

World.title: Disputes Tribunal orders Kmart to pay Christchurch couple over contaminated sand
World.content:
Kmart has been ordered to pay thousands to a Christchurch couple whose toddlers played with asbestos-contaminated sand.

Last year, the retail giant was part of a nationwide recall of coloured play sand products, after they tested positive for tremolite - a form of asbestos associated with higher cancer risks at low exposure levels.

Elle Chrisp and David Dingwall took Kmart to the Disputes Tribunal, seeking re-imbursement for costs associated with asbestos contamination and future medical monitoring.

The Christchurch pair claimed $60,000 in total.

In a recent decision, the tribunal ordered Kmart to pay the family $15,185.42 to cover costs associated with asbestos testing and remediation.

It found the play sand purchased was unsafe, not fit for purpose and not of acceptable quality under the Consumer Guarantees Act.

Referee Cynthia Hawes said the sand should not have been offered for sale.

"I do not think that any reasonable parent, acquainted with the fact that the moulding sand contained asbestos, and regardless of the quantity or proportion in the sand, would purchase it for his or her child to play with."

The claim for medical expenses was not allowed.

A Kmart spokesperson said the product recall was part of a broader industry issue.

"When the matter became known to us, we acted quickly by removing affected products from sale, issuing recall notices, and supporting customers with refunds and guidance on safely disposing of the products based on regulatory advice."

They said the company was reviewing the tribunal's decision.

Consumer NZ head of research and advocacy Gemma Rasmussen said Chrisp and Dingwall spent months gathering evidence, and forked out thousands of dollars to take Kmart to the Disputes Tribunal.

She said the ruling found "firmly in the family's favour".

"It is completely reasonable for them to undertake everything that they did from testing to vacating their home, and Kmart should have to pay for that."

Rasmussen said the ruling did not set a precedent, but it sent a clear message and she hoped other families were encouraged to make claims.

However, she said the order ultimately showed the difficulty in getting redress following a product safety failure.

She said current laws were too reactive and regulatory reform was needed.

"Our market place has dramatically changed from major retailers like Kmart selling thousands of goods to people shopping on platforms like Temu and Ali Express, and we really need the government to take this a little more seriously."

World.title: Health NZ says cervical screening IT doesn't need overhaul
World.content:
Health New Zealand believes the technology behind its failure-prone cervical screening register is largely OK - but not entirely.

The register that was rushed in three years ago failed to trigger almost a million notifications to women about cancer screening.

Experts who investigated the problems last year told HNZ in February to look at whether the register's IT platform was viable and, if not, find other tech.

The agency's action plan says it will both assess and enhance the tech.

HNZ told RNZ it began that work in June.

"We are confident that the programme's IT system is generally fit for purpose, although we recognise there is work to do to ensure that invitations to screen are generated for all women that should get them," said national prevention screening director Alana Ewe-Snow.

"In short, we anticipate improvement to the current IT system, not an overhaul."

All 48 recommendations, including the tech to improve the system, would be completed within two years and it was monitoring for any harm meantime, HNZ said. No harm had been found.

Women's health advocates said the register failure was "appalling" and workforce churn, including at the tech level, had contributed to it.

As a result of the national screening unit being shut down as a standalone agency, data analysts had been shifted to HNZ's digital services side, helping create "exactly the kind of workforce churn that our organisations warned would be a recipe for disaster", said the Auckland Women's Health Council, Federation of Women's Health Councils and the Cartwright Collective in a statement.

The register was built to store cervical screening test results, track screening paths - how often women should be screened, according to risk - and send out notifications, including recalls, reminders and invitations to women.

Despite the failures, it had boosted screening numbers from just under 10 percent in 2023 to 77 percent in 2026, Ewe-Snow said.

"The register is working well for most women, so there is no intention to start again.

"We know, however, we have more work to do tighten the register to ensure invitations are getting sent to all eligible women."

The action plan says: "This includes enhancing digital and technology foundations."

Its launch in September 2023 was rushed, and HNZ knew it had limited functions and several problems, including incomplete data, yet did not monitor it properly after it went live, the expert investigation report's 118 pages found.

It was sending out only a couple of hundred notifications a week, instead of the expected few thousand.

By April 2024, an internal report showed the register's design was not up to expectations and the tech's 'logic' system "was not built as intended". Poor data quality made it worse.

That sparked the external review, done by mid-2025, although its report was released only this month, after reporting by Stuff.

"We are deeply concerned by reports that nurses and other frontline staff have said they tried to raise the alarm about these failings before the system went live," said the women's health advocates.

Initially, the project contract was signed in 2019, with Deloitte using software from Salesforce, although actual work began in 2022. By early 2023, it still needed funding.

The goalposts on technical requirements were shifted, as the screening platform was being built.

"The register is not yet functioning as a comprehensive clinical safety net," the review said in 2025, after 18 months of work trying to fix it.

It was, however, working "satisfactorily in many ways".

The advocates noted the failures included no screening histories properly transitioned onto the new register; and a "concerning level" of clinical risk around recommendation mismatches between screening laboratories and the register.

The experts gave Health NZ a list of five things to do on the tech front.

It "must critically assess the long-term viability of the register and the underlying National Screening Solution [NSS]", they said in February.

It needed to know from the IT supplier if and when this could be done, and at what cost - and if not, change tack.

"If this assessment determines that the required functionality cannot be implemented, a risk-assessment should be undertaken of procuring a new software solution in the long term, rather than continuing with the register and NSS."

Ewe-Snow said they began that in June, "assessing how the technology that sits in behind the register can be improved", and this was ongoing, although a timeline was not yet finalised.

"We need to be alert to opportunities for further improvement, especially in a world where technology is changing rapidly."

World.title: Cook Strait ferry sailings cancelled due to heavy swells
World.content:
Ferry services in the Cook Strait are cancelling crossings due to heavy swells on Tuesday.

A strong southerly wind is bringing large swells and gusts.

Interislander services between Picton and Wellington at 9.30am, 3.30pm and 9.30pm were cancelled on Tuesday, as well as the 3.30am on Wednesday 19 August.

"Safety is our priority and we only sail when it is safe to do so," said Interislander.

It said passengers would be contacted and rebooked to a different service.

Bluebridge has cancelled sailings between Wellington and Picton at 1.30pm.

World.title: More will die in prison if mental health bed shortage continues - Ombudsman
World.content:
Warning: This story contains references to suicide.

More people will die in prison if a shortage of beds in forensic mental health facilities continues, the Chief Ombudsman is warning.

The Ombudsman's briefing to Parliament's health select committee said mentally unwell and intellectually disabled people were increasingly being imprisoned rather than hospitalised due to the bed shortage.

It was a longstanding issue but had shifted from isolated cases to a frequent pattern, and prisons were not equipped to support people who should be in hospital, the report said.

Chief Ombudsman John Allen told RNZ he recently visited a unit at Auckland's Mount Eden prison which held people who were mentally distressed.

"While I was at the prison, a person within a similar unit committed suicide," he said.

"So the pressure is real."

It was made worse with the growth in prison populations, Allen said.

"It is a problem now, it is a problem that is growing, and it's a problem that if we turn away from it, is going to create very bad outcomes for people within that community."

The Ombudsman reviewed 60 deaths in custody over a three-year period, and more than a third (22 cases) were suspected suicides.

Of those, 14 people had been referred to forensic mental health services "at some point during their time in custody", and eight had engaged with forensic services.

However five were declined because they did not meet the criteria, and two should have been referred but were not.

True demand unknown

Up to 50 people at any one time were in prison waiting for a forensic mental health placement, and some of them were on remand - awaiting trial while not having been convicted of a crime.

Some were untreated while they were waiting, because compulsory treatment cannot be provided in prison, the briefing said - so people can refuse the medication.

Allen told RNZ that resulted in "real disasters" - people harming themselves or others.

"And when you have a system where people are now being double bunked because the prisons simply aren't able to accommodate the population growth, you can imagine that that complicates it even further," he said.

The briefing said the true demand for specialist help was unknown.

Mental Health Minister Matt Doocey said the last two Budgets put $86 million into specialist forensic mental health services. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Sometimes court orders to send people to specialist facilities were not made, because it was known that no beds were available.

"Data only shows people admitted, not people who should have been admitted," it said.

Allen said the purpose of the briefing was to put it on MPs' radars.

"Mental health and vulnerable people and prison populations are not necessarily the vote catchers in the political system, but they are some of the most vulnerable people within our society," he said.

"It's to encourage our Parliament as a whole, to take a long-term approach to the development of appropriate infrastructure, appropriate training for staff to address this problem over time."

Bed shortfall expected to grow

Health NZ said the country was currently short 36 forensic mental health beds, and that would grow to 137 by 2035 if no further capacity was added.

Mental Health Minister Matt Doocey said the last two Budgets put $86 million into specialist forensic mental health services.

That included 20 forensic mental health beds - 14 for inpatients, and six "step-down" beds which help people transition from inpatient services back into the community.

"Reports like this reflect exactly why I am committed to ensuring faster access to support, opening more beds, and growing the front-line workforce," Doocey said.

Health NZ specialist mental health and addiction director Karla Bergquist said it was working with the Ministry of Health and Corrections to improve access to forensic mental health services.

"This includes work to provide ministers with options to address short- to medium-term capacity constraints, alongside immediate actions to improve safety and support for people in prison who require a secure hospital bed," she said.

"The goal is to ensure people receive timely, co-ordinated forensic mental health care in the most appropriate setting."

Corrections chief mental health and addictions officer Dr Emma Gardner said prisons were not designed to support people with serious mental illness, but Corrections was doing all it could to support people's mental wellbeing, ensure physical safety, and to treat them with dignity and respect.

"We are often required to manage some of New Zealand's most unwell people in a custodial environment," she said.

"This can be extremely challenging for our frontline staff who do an incredible job working with often volatile and vulnerable people."

Corrections was upskilling staff to help them manage people's needs and keep them safe, and had dedicated mental health staff in all prisons, she said.

World.title: A spotlight on the little guys - what small businesses want from government
World.content:
Small businesses say they don't want handouts - but they do want stability, both economically and in government policy

Rotorua Chamber chief executive Melanie Short makes no bones about how tough life is for small businesses these days.

"In the last fortnight, we've had three hospo businesses go out of business and a contracting business.

"As one of the businesses that went into receivership last week said, everything was fine - until it wasn't."

Her concern hit the headlines, when she asked the prime minister about how long struggling local businesses could hang on, given rising costs and fewer customers.

Christopher Luxon's answer really put the spotlight on the issue for all the wrong reasons. He later apologised, but his perceived lack of empathy was also a factor in the leadership coup against him last week.

Today on The Detail, we look at how small businesses have a big impact - and ask what they want from a government.

Short says the Rotorua Chamber is apolitical and she doesn't want to relitigate last week's controversy, but the data from the organisation's latest business pulse survey painted a picture of a decent drop in business confidence - the sharpest drop seen over the last nine years they've been running the survey.

"Also, as you would expect, the affordability of doing business was also impacted.

"Our businesses in Rotorua are resilient and quite innovative, but at the same time, it's been quite a long period of time and we've had to put our all into everything. We're just looking for some stability, some improvement... and we're hearing that's coming, but right now, we're feeling a bit tired by it all."

It's been a long Covid hangover for businesses in this tourist town.

"We've had the impact of Covid, we've been through recessions, emergency housing, etc... so we continue to re-invent ourselves, but I guess the question was, 'When is this improvement coming?'

"We know there's a whole lot of external factors that we have to deal with as well, as a country. We get that, but the message that we want any party to hear at the moment is that, you know, we want to be listened to, we want to be talked to about the various issues we're having and we just want to be heard."

New Zealand is a nation of little guys. More than 97 percent of firms employ fewer than 20 workers and we have more than 600,000 enterprises.

They collectively employ nearly 30 percent of NZ's total private workforce.

In the year to March 2026, 3023 companies were placed into liquidation, even more than last year's 15-year high. Liquidations have climbed more than 70 percent over three years.

At the same time, in the year to July, more than 62,000 companies were incorporated - the highest number in five years.

Several financial commentators have said many people are effectively buying themselves a job, possibly after being made redundant, and some of the new formation numbers are just ownership changes.

Stats NZ data indicates just 27 percent of small-to-medium enterprises established in 2015 were still in business in 2025.

Advocacy for Business NZ director Catherine Beard tells The Detail that, while things have been tough, we are starting to see better indicators coming through.

The latest monthly performance and manufacturing index shows things picking up, "which is encouraging".

"We know that, in tough times, bigger businesses are more resilient, they tend to weather the storm better, and smaller businesses do find it more difficult."

While small businesses make up a massive part of the economy, Beard says they probably don't feel they have the corresponding heft, when it comes to getting into the ear of politicians.

She says Business NZ is acting on a report it did on what's keeping small businesses awake at night and is rating various government agencies on how they're doing to solve these problems.

That includes health and safety regulations, finding their way around immigration regulations to bring in specialist staff and employment agreements.

"Everything around hiring and firing for small businesses can be problematic, because they just don't have the internal resources, they don't have internal HR, they don't have internal legal."

Beard says, in spite of our country having a reputation for being easy to do business in, she believes that's a bit of a myth - and while it's easy to register a new company, dealing with the regulatory complexity is difficult.

She says business say they don't want government handouts, but they do want stability - in the economy, and in government policy.

World.title: Golf course in court as parklands protesters take on SA government
World.content:
In what's been described as a David and Goliath battle, a trial has begun in the Federal Court, with two South Australians challenging the state government's redevelopment of the North Adelaide golf course.

Public servant Edwin Kemp Attrill and Kaurna Arabana woman Janette Milera are challenging the redevelopment, arguing it is in breach of federal conservation laws.

In front of other protesters opposed to the parklands project outside court, Mr Kemp Attrill said the unfolding legal process was "very nerve-wracking".

"It's a big uphill battle for us but we're really proud to be standing here," he said.

Ms Milera said she was taking action because she thought it was the right thing to do.

"This case is about respecting cultural tradition and truth telling," she said.

For [SA Premier] Peter [Malinauskas], it's a new golf course. For me, it's a bloodline.

"This case we're doing is because the parklands belong to the people and they need to be protected."

Protesters opposed to the state government's actions in the Adelaide parklands gathered outside the Federal Court. (ABC News: Leah MacLennan)

The state government announced its plan to redevelop and expand the golf course, as part of its bid to move the LIV Golf tournament into the city.

It said 585 trees would be cut down in the process, to be replaced with new plantings.

The state government passed laws earlier this year, taking control of that part of the parklands away from the Adelaide City Council, to allow it to go ahead with the redevelopment.

But the removal of trees sparked protests and the legal action taken by Mr Kemp Attrill and Ms Milera.

The redevelopment of the North Adelaide course has involved the felling of hundreds of trees. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

In his opening address, the lawyer for the pair, Arturo Dal Cin, told the court the Adelaide parklands were given national heritage listing in 2008.

He said more than 400 trees had already cut down at the golf course — a number he said accounted for 15 per cent of all the trees in the area marked for the first stage of the development.

"Recognition of parklands necessarily includes recognition of established trees, because a necessary element of parklands is established, mature trees," Mr Dal Cin said.

He said the works have impacted the national heritage values of the parklands.

"A fundamental issue in this case, one of the fundamental issues, is the extent to which your Honour finds the removal of trees to this scale to be a significant impact on what the appellants will be contending is a national heritage value — namely the parklands and their protection," he said.

Trees were removed from the area in May. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Mr Dal Cin said evidence would also be presented during the trial about the impact on Aboriginal cultural heritage and on local flying fox populations.

'Assault on democracy'

Before going to court, government lawyers wrote to Mr Kemp Attrill, warning him he could be liable for $4 million in costs if he lost.

Outside court, Mr Kemp Attrill said the government had not backed down.

"It's really concerning to us that in a public interest case the government has continued to say that they will essentially crush us if they win," he said.

"We think that's incredibly unfair and it's an assault on democracy in South Australia."

Mr Kemp Attrill had submitted an affidavit to the court saying he was "shocked" when he saw the loss of trees.

On cross-examination, he was shown aerial pictures of the course before and after the tree removal.

Crown lawyer Alison Doecke KC asked if a significant number of trees remained in the parklands following the works.

"I put to you that when one has regard to the aerial view, it is very hard to identify where the trees have been removed," she said.

"From the two photographs, yes," Mr Kemp Attrill said.

He said he often walks his dog around the golf course at night, and he has noticed the loss of trees.

"Walking around the perimeter, you can notice there's more sky," he said.

The redevelopment of the course was announced as part of plans for LIV Golf. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Ms Doecke suggested to Mr Kemp Attrill that "the significant change in the appearance of the site is because of the removal of the grass, not the removal of the trees. Do you accept that?" she said.

"No, as I said, it was noticeable as soon as the trees were removed; the view was different," Mr Kemp Attrill said.

"Standing outside the fence, if you're not right up against the fence you actually don't see the grass, you can only see the trees, and that was a noticeable difference."

But when asked by Ms Doecke if he would concede "there's still an awful lot of trees on the site", Mr Kemp Attrill said "yes".

Speaking at a media conference, Premier Peter Malinauskas said his government has acted lawfully.

"All the advice that I've received from the relevant agencies is they've sought to comply with all requirements as they've gone through it," he said.

" I've said all along that any individual is welcome to take up their rights to challenge things in court, as is being done in this particular instance. "

The trial is expected to take five days, with government lawyers to present their response on Wednesday.

World.title: Sydney Swans CEO confirms police investigating alleged incident 'involving several players'
World.content:
The Sydney Swans have confirmed several of their footballers were involved in an "alleged incident" in Melbourne last night.

The Swans issued a statement just after midday today.

"The Swans have notified the AFL and relevant authorities and cannot provide further comment at this stage," the club said.

Victoria Police separately issued a statement saying detectives were investigating a report of a sexual assault in East Melbourne.

The Sydney Swans stayed at the Pullman in East Melbourne last night. (ABC News)

"The incident occurred at a hotel on Wellington Parade in the early hours of the morning," a spokesperson said.

"The exact circumstances are yet to be established, and the investigation into the incident remains ongoing."

Sydney Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich called a press conference this afternoon that lasted less than one minute.

"We're still piecing together exactly what's transpired here and have our own set of internal inquiries ongoing," he said.

"Safe to say, we're extremely shocked and disappointed that this has taken place and that the players have found themselves in this situation.

"We understand the level of interest in the matter, and there's going to be lots of speculation, but given it's a police matter right now, that's all that we can say."

Matthew Pavlich addressed the media this afternoon. (ABC News)

The AFL released a brief statement.

"The club made the AFL aware of the matter which is currently under Victoria Police investigation," the statement read.

NSW Police Minister Yasmin Catley said she was unaware of the details of the allegations, but she was confident Victorian authorities would take them "very seriously."

"We have to be mindful of the fact that the alleged offences occurred in a different jurisdiction. So, they [Victoria Police] will be leading that investigation," she said.

Asked if she would be seeking a briefing from police herself given it was a high-profile case allegedly involving Sydney-based AFL players, she said: "The police will definitely lead on that" and "brief me accordingly".

"The investigation is underway, I think we should let the police do their work in Victoria, and the NSW police will let me know if I need to know anything."

The Swans were staying in Melbourne overnight after their 36-point win over Essendon at the MCG yesterday.

Sydney is sitting in second spot on the AFL ladder heading into the final round of the 2026 season, with the finals due to start within weeks.

The team has had 17 wins this season and is due to play its next game at home at the SCG against North Melbourne.

World.title: No smiles as Chris O'Connell advances, while Aussie women's campaign ends
World.content:
Chris O'Connell and Adam Walton have made it four Australian men in the third round of the Cincinnati Master, while Talia Gibson's loss to Aryna Sabalenka left the women's draw without green and gold representation.

Gibson was beaten 6-2, 7-6(7/2) by the world number one in an hour and 52 minutes, while O'Connell and Walton joined Alex de Minaur and Rinky Hijikata in the round of 32.

But O'Connell was in no mood to celebrate after progressing thanks to an injury retirement by 11th-seeded opponent Casper Ruud.

The Australian qualifier picked up his fourth win in five days at the Masters 1000 tournament in what is proving his most profitable week of the season, but there were no smiles as he sympathised with Norway's three-time grand slam finalist on his concerning retirement after 64 minutes play.

Ruud had started well, moving into a 5-2 lead in the opening set, but the Sydneysider powered back to take the first set, sealing it 7-5 with an ace, as Ruud began to look in increasing discomfort with a back problem.

With Ruud leading the second set 2-1 on serve, the Norwegian world number 17 stretched for a wide serve and immediately decided enough was enough, going to the net to offer his hand to the Aussie.

Clearly with one eye on the US Open, where the main draw starts a week on Sunday, 2022 Flushing Meadows runner-up Ruud was not keen to take any risks.

For world number 129 O'Connell, it was the continuation of an excellent spell following his first-round victory over Poland's world number 68 Kamil Majchrzak.

He will next meet Brazilian teenage superstar Joao Fonseca, who defeated Botic van de Zandschulp 6-4, 7-6(7/2), and victory in that match would push O'Connell back to the verge of the world's top 100.

Talia Gibson's loss to Aryna Sabalenka leaves no Australian women in the Cincinnati singles draw. (Getty Images: Robert Prange)

Walton made it four Australians through to the third round along with Hijikata, who faces Jakub Mensik, and national number one Alex de Minaur, who meets British Wimbledon hero Arthur Fery.

Walton, the 27-year-old Queenslander currently ranked 98 in the world, overcame the 29th-seeded Peruvian Ignacio Buse 6-4, 6-3 in 72 minutes to set up a showdown with either American Ben Shelton, the eighth seed, or Jaime Faria of Portugal.

World.title: After constant chopping and changing, Green goes 'back to what worked'
World.content:
Cameron Green has delivered for a shell-shocked Australian side to give himself breathing space at number five, leading captain Pat Cummins to predict a long stint in one position in the batting line-up.

Green's 104 in the second innings of the nine-wicket loss to Bangladesh in Darwin was his first in Australia and also broke an 11-innings run without passing the half-century mark.

The 27-year-old all-rounder has been heavily criticised in Australian cricket for not turning his undoubted potential into results.

But his knock in the loss means he leaves the Northern Territory as one of the only Aussie batters who can hold their heads high, with Cummins "not too sure" on the best course of action to turn things around before the second Test starts in Mackay on Saturday.

Shock loss to Bangladesh reveals Aussie cracks On paper, Australia's full-strength team should have wiped the floor with Bangladesh. But a lack of application to their Test match craft has left Australia vulnerable to teams that are driven to succeed in the longest format.

"We're always quite individual, everyone goes about it slightly differently, so coaches will work with each player individually," he said.

"I don't think there was a huge trend, everyone got out a little bit differently, but I think it's pretty clear it's not quite functioning as well as we'd like as a group.

"If we need to make some changes to our style, we've got a week or so, we better do it pretty quickly."

Cummins said before the Test that Green had been encouraged to "intimidate" and he did it the way he knows best, driving with commanding power and poise while accumulating runs at a steady rate without taking risks.

It is a method that has worked in Sheffield Shield cricket and he showcased why Test selectors have persevered with him despite the outside noise calling for his head.

Green's third Test century did not lead to a win but that was largely due to the failure of the rest of the order to stay with him in good batting conditions on the third and fourth days.

Australia will consider making changes to the underperforming top order for the second Test in Mackay that starts on Saturday, but Green will be one of the first picked.

"I'm sure he will get an extended run somewhere," Cummins said when asked if Green had tied down the number five position.

"I thought he was really impressive and controlled his innings. He looked in total command of his skills out there. He just needed one or two of us to bat alongside him."

Green and Steve Smith were the only Australian batters who could be happy with their output. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Green struggled in the last Ashes series, as many batters did, making just 171 runs at an average of 24.42 after being moved around from fifth to eighth in the order.

He earlier did a solid job on the West Indies tour, averaging 30.66 at first drop as the only member of the top three to average more than 20 across the three Tests.

"We obviously think very highly of Cam," Cummins said.

"The last Ashes series probably didn't go as well as he would have liked but before that on the West Indian tour he was probably our best batter in really tough circumstances when he was batting a little higher.

"It was great for him to go out there and show the rest of the world how good he is."

Quick hits as Bangladesh wraps up famous win Litton Das was wrong-footed behind the stumps, and Mehidy Hasan Miraz suffered a worse fate in front of them. Here are the quick hits from day four of the first Test between Australia and Bangladesh.

Green was fortunate in the final session on the third day when an inside edge off Taskin Ahmed grazed his leg stump on the way to the boundary.

The bails were not dislodged and the all-rounder dug in and made the most of his reprieve.

Green told Fox Cricket after his knock that he had approached his innings against Bangladesh like he used to do "back in the day".

"I think I've just been chopping and changing a little bit recently, so it's nice just to go back to what worked," Green said.

"It has been a long couple of months so it is nice to get a few rewards for it."

As for the critics, Green said it just came with the territory.

"I feel like there are always wolves when you are playing Test cricket. When you play for Australia, you always have to perform," he said.

World.title: Aussie star Lani Pallister ends American GOAT's 16-year win streak
World.content:
Lani Pallister has toppled swimming legend Katie Ledecky for a second time in 24 hours to complete her stunning Pan Pacific championship campaign with a fourth gold medal.

The 24-year-old Pallister was under world-record pace for much of the race as she won the 800m freestyle final in eight minutes and 6.1 seconds from four-time Olympic champion Ledecky (8:07.26) in the American's signature event.

Ledecky's lone previous defeat in an 800m freestyle final since 2010 came in a small domestic event in February 2024 against Canadian superstar Summer McIntosh, making Pallister the first to beat her over the distance at an international meet.

"Today is the most nervous I've ever felt in my entire life. I was just so locked in and I've been really focused on what I want," Pallister said.

"The 800m is my favourite event. So to have the three titles this week and be just behind Katie in the 1,500 [is great but] … this is the one that I wanted."

Ledecky, who famously signed an autograph for a young Pallister a decade ago, telling her to "dream big", wrote on Instagram that she "can't help but smile about another incredible race with [Pallister]".

Ledecky (right) told a young Pallister to "dream big". (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

Pallister had beaten Ledecky to win the 400m freestyle gold a day earlier and took silver behind her great rival in the 1,500m free, as well as downed McIntosh to win the 200m free gold and also collect gold in the 4x200m free relay.

Australia's Dolphins well and truly flexed their middle- and long-distance muscle at the meet, two years out from the LA Olympics, with Sam Short also emerging with three individual gold medals after winning the men's 1,500m free to go with his 400 and 800 free titles.

Having beaten Ian Thorpe's 1999 Pan Pacs record to win the 400m, he erased another Australian legend's mark in the 1,500m.

His time of 14:33.97 was the sixth-fastest in history, breaking Grant Hackett's Australian record that had stood since 2001, and came a day after German teenager Johannes Liebmann smashed the world record at the European Aquatics Championships.

Loading Instagram content

"I am proud of my consistency," said Short, who also won the 400m, 800m, and 1,500m titles at the Commonwealth Games late last month.

"I've gone five well sub-15-minute swims now, so if I can do that here my average come Olympics, world championships, all I need to do is be my average and be contending for some podium places."

Adding to a strong final day for Australia, Zac Stubblety-Cook went from fourth to first in the 200m breaststroke final, winning in 2:08.09 from American Josh Matheny.

And countryman Jamie Jack won the 50m freestyle gold in a championship record of 21.35 as American Jack Alexy took silver in 21.42.

"It's awesome. That's the best I could ask for," Jack said.

American Kate Douglass lowered her own world record in the 50m free twice, winning the final in 23.19.

Douglass capped a busy night by anchoring the US women to a dominant victory in the 4x100 medley relay in a championship record time of 3:50.43, with Australia second in 3:55.09.

The US men won from Australia in the 4x100 medley relay.

Australia finished the four-day meet with a medal haul of 15 gold, 11 silver and nine bronze, behind only the US haul of 19, 22 and nine.
